speechtext:

As the Minister of Finance has managed to maintain simultaneously both that economic conditions are favourable at the present for an end to controls and that the decontrol process may not begin for another year, would he now try to make some contribution toward clarifying his position? First, can he tell the House whether he will ask the provinces to renew their anti-inflation program agreements when they expire this April; and, if he

will ask for a renewal, can he tell the House for how long a period he will suggest that the contracts ought to be renewed?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have asked the provinces to continue their participation. In the meantime a group representative of several government of Canada departments will be calling on the provinces for the purpose of discussing the provisions which we set before the meeting last week and seeking their support in particular for a general agreement in which the private sector would participate to restrain inflationary expectations after controls.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF RENEWAL OF AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES- COMPOSITION OF GROUP MEETING WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF RENEWAL OF AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES- COMPOSITION OF GROUP MEETING WITH PROVINCES

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, considering that the minister said on January 24 at the Canadian Club in Toronto that "we need to see further progress in reducing the rate of inflation" before ending controls and then one week later on February 1 said that there now seems to be a green light for decontrol, what has happened in the economic situation which now leads him to believe this is a proper time to go ahead with decontrols?

speechtext: As well as the minister's suggestions on January 24 and February 1, the minister also said, adding to the confusion of the situation, that perhaps controls could last well into 1978, does the minister believe, seeing that he has now said that the situation in economic terms is favourable for decontrol, we will have precisely the same economic conditions in 1978 as we have today?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON NEW METHOD OF COLLECTING STATISTICS ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Since Statistics Canada excludes from its determination of monthly unemployment levels all those who have not looked for work since leaving their last job, and since such a method seriously understates the real level of unemployment in Canada, particularly in regions of persistently high unemployment, will the minister undertake to investigate this situation immediately and bring forward a new method of collecting unemployment figures which more accurately reflects reality?

Of course, the question of the scientific methods of assessing the unemployment level in Canada is extemely complex and I think we can argue at length on that matter. The hon. member might think that the questions are not put in a satisfactory manner, but a large part of the Canadian public also think that the questions are put so as to reflect a higher unemployment rate than the actual rate. This matter may be debated at length. subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITIES IN QUEBEC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Solicitor General.

Over the weekend, information media reported that the government plans to build four federal buildings to be used as penitentiaries in Quebec. Can the minister tell the House whether the construction of those penitentiaries is due to the fact that the number of clients in that field is increasing or to the fact that buildings now used to this end have become so dilapidated as to be non-usable?

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITIES IN QUEBEC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course we have across Canada a penitentiary building construction program which takes several factors into consideration. One of these is the federal government's wish to finally close down some old institutions and, seeing the hon. member speaks of the province of Quebec, one of the reasons why we wish to build additional facilities is to allow us to close down what is commonly known as the "old pen". As the "old pen" has cells for over 400 prisoners, and as we intend to build new prisons taking into account the most modern concepts of penal science, we intend to build institutions for a maximum of 185 to 200 inmates. Now, the wish to close down the "old pen" at St. Vincent-de-Paul in addition to the need to face the increase in the number of prisoners, which goes up by about 3 per cent each year but which last year in Quebec went up by almost three times the national average, force us to build new penitentiaries in that area.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITIES IN QUEBEC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question?
Given his positive answer, could the minister tell the House which sites and locations are being considered for the erection of these buildings and also how many inmates each one of these buildings will house?

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF NEW FACILITIES IN QUEBEC-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are considering buildings which would house around 185 inmates in medium security penitentiaries and about 196 inmates in maximum security penitentiaries. Concerning the selection of sites where these penitentiaries will be erected in Quebec, we are now considering a whole list of possible locations and I hope to be able to make a final decision in four to six weeks from now.

Mr. Chairman, clause 57 of the bill deals with the registered home ownership savings plan.
And other things.

I want to make some comments about this provision in the Income Tax Act. A few years ago in a budget the government introduced a provision to stimulate home building and assist young couples and lower income people to save in order that they might build a new home. The government hoped to accomplish this end with the registered home ownership savings plan. Under the plan a person would register and be able to contribute $1,000 per year to a maximum of $10,000 in ten years. That $1,000 set aside under the registered home ownership savings plan was to be tax free, as was the interest earned by moneys deposited under the plan. In other words, the moneys diverted into such a plan would never be taxed. When you look at the program and how it has been working, you find that as of 1974, the last year for which I have statistics available, some $65 million of tax savings were allowed through this registered home ownership savings plan.
The concept of helping Canadians to save in order to purchase a house is one with which all members of this House of Commons are in agreement. The government, looking at its record of housing in Canada, has something to be ashamed of in terms of the cost of housing today because of the high interest rates it has tolerated, especially in terms of mortgages that low and middle income people have to pay. The policy of this government in so far as adequately housing Canadians is concerned is something that I deplore, considering how many Canadians today are ill-sheltered.
If, in order to help Canadians build houses, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs were to stand in the House and announce that he would provide a cash grant to Canadians based on terms that the more you earn, the greater your grant, all of us in the opposition would be indignant at the unfairness of such a program. The public at large would have great objection and great difficulty trying to fathom why, the more you made in terms of income, the greater the house buying grant the government would give you.
When we look at this clause of the bill which has to do with the Income Tax Act and how it operates in terms of RHOSPs, we Find that is the very principle with which we are dealing. In other words, the greater your income, the higher you are on the income ladder, the greater the tax benefit will be for you if you subscribe to a registered home ownership savings plan. That is what we in the New Democratic Party so strongly object to, namely, that his plan, like many of the other provisions, benefits wealthy Canadians more than lower and middle income Canadians for whom the plan was supposedly designed to help in the first place.
Looking at the figures from Statistics Canada and how the various income groups have been able to benefit from the registered home ownership savings plan, we find that if a person's income was under $2,000-and this would only apply
February 7, 1977

to people on pensions, disability pensions and so on-their average saving under this plan was $105. If we move up the income-ladder to those earning between $2,000 and $5,000 a year, we see that their saving under this plan would be about $203. For the income group between $5,000 and $10,000, their tax saving would be about $264. Notice that as we go up the income ladder the tax saving increases. For those earning between $10,000 and $15,000 a year, the average saving is about $309. For people earning between $15,000 and $20,000 a year, their average saving is $365. For people earning between $20,000 and $50,000 a year, the saving under this plan would average $462. For those earning over $50,000 a year, the average saving would be $571.
Rather than providing a kind of tax structure through this home ownership savings plan to help those who need help the most to Find decent accommodation through home ownership, the plan works in the reverse direction. I agree there would be some saving to lower and middle income Canadians, but it gives a far greater saving to upper income Canadians whom we assume have greater ability to afford housing than low income Canadians. That is unfair.
Looking at the way the savings are proportioned among the different income groups, I ask the minister what is fair about a home ownership savings plan for the income group between $5,000 and $10,000 a year when only one in 49 taxpayers was able to take advantage of it. For someone earning between $10,000 and $15,000 a year, one in 32 was able to take advantage of the program, and for those earning over $50,000, one in 16 was able to take advantage of it. I refer not only to the amount of money one can save under the plan, as I illustrated by earlier figures-the more you make, the greater it is-but in terms of who is taking advantage of the plan we find, again, it is upper income Canadians, those we would assume to have the means to buy a house, who benefit the most.
These are the people who are taking advantage of the plan in terms of numbers and who are also gaining the greatest benefit in terms of dollars. This plan, like the registered retirement savings plan and the child care deduction provisions which we criticized earlier, provides disproportionate advantages to upper income Canadians. For that reason, we strenuously object to it.
If the government is serious about providing adequate housing for Canadians, there should be a cut-off limit, in terms of income, as to whether you qualify for this plan or, better still, a tax credit formula so that low and middle income Canadians who most need help will be able to get the dollars savings that one would assume a fair income tax system would provide.
On the whole, when we look at this gimmick, this registered home ownership plan as a tool to help Canadians find adequate housing falls far short of the goal. We are, unfortunately, facing a tremendous problem of high unemployment. Officially, the rate run at about 7 per cent, but very likely, because of inadequate statistical methods, this figure does not repre-
Income Tax Act
sent the true position which is probably around 11 per cent- 800,000 or one million Canadian are out of work. If the aim is to get these Canadians back to work as well as to provide decent shelter for the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who need it, we should not rely upon these tax gimmicks; there should be a massive investment of public money in a national housing program to stimulate home construction. Not only would this get many unemployed Canadians back to work, but we would begin to provide a housing stock adequate for the needs of many Canadian families who are presently living in slums or near-slums.
Another way in which the government could help solve the housing crisis would be by regulating mortgage interest rates either through the Bank of Canada or through the budgetary process. We in this party have suggested that the government instruct the commercial banks to set aside a certain portion of their capital to provide mortgages, at 6 per cent to low income families deserving of such assistance. If we brought down high mortgage rates we would do more to stimulate home construction than by introducing the kind of gimmick represented by RHOSPs.
It must be disillusioning for Canadians to face the mortgage payments they are required to make today. Over the weekend I was talking to a constituent who had taken out a $40,000 mortgage at 10'/2 per cent. He had received an annual statement from the bank which showed he had reduced his mortgage over the past year by some $400. But his interest payments amounted to around $4,000. When a family is burdened with mortgage payments on that scale, is it any wonder that in so many cases both spouses need to work?
Not only does the RHOSP benefit the wrong group, that is, those in the upper income brackets who have a better chance of coping with housing costs, but it does not begin to come to grips with the housing crisis. I am concerned, also, about the loopholes in this plan. In theory it is supposed to help people save toward the purchase of a house. But the provisions are so loose that money can be paid into the plan and used later to buy furniture. Use can be made of it as a tax dodge, and at the end of ten years there is no need to buy a house at all; the money accumulated, say $10,000 plus interest, can be transferred to an RRSP so as to avoid taxation.
Even in cases where a person already owns a house, the fund can be transferred to a spouse and the spouse will qualify under the plan. There are various provisions which make it possible to transfer these funds into RRSPs, and so on- all in all, a loophole big enough to drive the family car through. In my opinion, the plan is poorly designed in relation to whom it helps and to what degree. I think it really amounts to a tax dodge available to the wealthy rather than a tax break to those who need it most. For this reason I strongly object to the way in which it is designed. We in the New Democratic Party would like to see it restructured as a tax credit and a limitation placed on its use. We want homes for lower and middle income Canadians.

I am obliged to the hon. member for his contribution. He talked about a family in his

February 7, 1977
Income Tax Act
riding, a family which, I take it, is typical in the sense that it is carrying a $40,000 mortgage and paying $4,000 or $5,000 a year on it. May I point out that this is exactly the kind of household which under RHOSP would be able to put money aside to provide a down payment on property. This measure will, in a substantial way, assist young people in particular who have entered the work force to set aside money to acquire property and make a home for themselves.
I think it is fair to remind the hon. member that this measure does not in any way exhaust the list of those the government has taken in the housing field. He would like to see a massive program of government spending in the housing area. Might I point out to him that this is exactly what was undertaken by the government in 1976 through various programs within the responsibility of my colleague, the Secretary of State for Urban Affairs. In round figures, $1.5 million was channelled by the federal government into programs concentrated mainly on those at the lower end of the income scale so as to make available one form of assistance or another, accounting for 120,000 of the 275,000 units of housing under way during 1976.
Incidentally, the figure of 275,000 units in that year was not only a record; it was well in excess of the target which had been set by my colleague. In that sense we have already witnessed a massive injection of money into the housing sector. I think, for example, of the Dundas-Sherbourne project in my own constituency. Federal funds represented about 95 per cent of the total cost in addition to the shared-cost of rental subsidies with the provincial government, and the result was the availability of accomodation in the downtown area for people in the lowest income groups who, but for this federal assistance, would not have such housing at all. In short, we are seeking to provide a spectrum of housing opportunities, and I think it is fair for me to comment that there has already been an effective and substantial addition to Canada's housing stock as a result of the programs to which I have referred.

Mr. Chairman, the minister started to recite some of the government's housing policies and programs, revelling in the 275,000 new units to be created. He would, of course, be the first to admit that there are some problems with the figures he recited. One of the major problems, which is evident to me from constituents who come to my office in Sault Ste. Marie, is the fact that of the many new houses that are built, most are priced beyond the family incomes of these people. In view of the actual cost of building a house and the cost of interest payments people are faced with today, the dream of owning a house is away beyond the reach of most. Not enough moderately-priced houses are being built.
Private developers, of course, can make a greater profit from the more expensive homes which upper income Canadians can afford, and this is the kind of home construction that is taking place all across Canada. Certainly, many more are built than the moderately-priced homes which the average Canadian would like to be able to afford. The government will probably

counter that argument by stating that there is the assisted home ownership plan, which again is a plan that in theory is very good but which in practice cuts out average income Canadians from any benefit. A ceiling is placed on the price of a house under which AHOP will grant a subsidy. For example, in Sault Ste. Marie there are just not enough moderately-priced houses on the market to qualify for AHOP assistance and provide a home for those with an income requirement to bring them within the program.
So although the government can trot out statistics showing the great work it is doing, the people whom I see from day to day who have problems finding adequate housing tell me a different story. They tell me the housing situation is not as rosy as the minister tries to make out. That is why I say that if this registered home ownership plan is to have any real benefit for those who need it the most, we will have to redesign it so that, in dollar terms and in terms of who can take most advantage of it, it is made available to low and middle income Canadians and not, as is presently the case, to help those in the upper income brackets.

what we are opposed to is what I would describe as consistent Liberal philosophy, that of not only assisting middle and upper income earners but richly rewarding them in terms of the provisions of this particular clause. That is all I have to say on that aspect. I still think that the real effect of these kinds of tax shelters on individual taxpayers has not been properly studied. If it has been properly studied, then in spite of its fundamental unfairness to those on low income, the principle has nevertheless been proceeded with.
I hope that the minister has read a document entitled "The Hidden Welfare System", produced by the national council of welfare, which analysed the personal income tax system. This particular provision came under very careful scrutiny and was heavily criticised in the report. It underlined the example that the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie so explicitly put before the committee-that of the plan's basic unfairness. It pointed out that the loss to the treasury as a result of these tax shelters is some $6.4 billion a year, and that if you took away those shelters every man, woman and child in Canada could be given $100 a month for the purpose of education, clothing or some basic and fundamental need. Yet the government continues to bring forward a system of reverse taxation.
1 could go into the question of the effect of this system on indexing, which makes it even more iniquitous. As a result of indexing we find that the value of these shelters to those of upper income is even greater. However, that is all 1 have to say on this clause, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not speak for any length of time, but I should like some clarification of clause 60 which unfortunately picks up some of the matters already dealt with in clause 43(3) on page 47 of the bill having to do with the definition of "charitable foundations", "charitable organizations", and so on. My question refers specifically to activities which are not necessarily related to the charity in question but are engaged in by a charitable organization or foundation, whichever is the case, in order to finance the further carrying on of their charitable work.
I am thinking, to be specific, of an operation such as a parking lot, the proceeds of which would be recoverable by the charitable foundation or organization to finance that charity's operation. There is another form of activity that a foundation or organization might be involved in, namely, the purchase of a building by way of investment in order to produce revenue which would assist the charitable organization or foundation in carrying on its work. I wonder whether the minister is in a position to say now whether any criteria are being used to determine which business activities would be permitted within the meaning of this bill as being eligible for tax exemption.
Income Tax Act

The hon. member has touched on one of the difficult questions involved in the exercise of reviewing the tax law as it affects charities. The basic purpose, going back to the common law, is that by definition a charity should not carry on a business, that it should engage primarily in the benevolent purposes for which it has been set up. But we all know that over a period of time, specifically for the purpose of augmenting the funds of charitable organizations, related businesses have been engaged in by the charities.
In my own city, the women's committee of the Ontario art gallery has been engaged in such activities, as have other charitable organizations; for example, in the preparing and sale of meals on the premises of the charitable organization as income earners for the particular charity. It is for that reason that subsection (j) has been added to try to define a little more clearly the question of related business.
The example given by the hon. member would not fit within the related business category, that is to say, the operation of a parking lot. Indeed, it is conceivable that it could be run by volunteers for the purpose of augmenting the income of the charitable organization; but that is not primarily what would be regarded as a related business. However, ultimately it is not for me to say: the definition of "related business" is included in the statute and it would be for the courts to interpret it. I should indicate, however, that from the extensive discussions that have been held with charitable organizations as a result of the study paper and the bill which was given first reading late last spring, and of this bill, the conclusion has been drawn that the introduction of the rules would not materially affect the existing operations of most charitable organizations and public foundations. This will be determined by the law. It may well be that there will be some activities which are not compatible with the carrying on of a charity which may fall afoul of this provision.

Mr. Chairman, I am not entirely satisfied. The minister has given some clarification, but the "related business" concept would have to be clarified by the courts. The courts have in front of them the wording of this bill. Presumably they would have, as well, any precedents established by court ruling. But this imposes upon charities a requirement to resort to legal action in order to resolve problems in which perhaps they had been involved for several years on the understanding, in the past, that these activities were recognized as legitimate businesses which would be carried on by those charitable organizations without implicating them in deeper tax commitments.
I notice that the minister spoke of the example of a parking lot operated by volunteers to raise money. Let us suppose that the parking lot happened to be in the same municipal area as a hospital, for example, and it was not volunteers but paid staff who were being employed in this operation; therefore it was a business with employees who are parking lot attendants being paid for their services. Would this further complicate their problem, or did the minister just throw in the word "volunteers" simply as one of the words that might be used with reference to persons running the parking lot?

February 7, 1977
Income Tax Act

The word "volunteer" is really a synonym for the definition in the latter part of clause 60(1 )(j). I should indicate that it is anticipated that where formerly a business of one kind or another was carried on by an existing charity, Revenue Canada would have no difficulty in defining those practices as being within the definition of a charitable operation. However, if a charity proposes to move into an activity which is competitive with commercial concerns, then at that point there has to be some question as to the appropriateness of its being allowed a charitable exemption.
If the charity, for example, is operating a business at a loss, it may have to make up the losses with its own funds, often out of amounts for which a tax deduction has been given. Businesses may become divorced from charity for practical purposes, their revenues being reinvested rather than going to the charity. The running of a business may become the principal focus of the charity's activity, with its charitable activites relegated to a secondary role. Obviously, between the incidental operation of the kind to which I referred, for example, the gallery or the hospital running a cafeteria, or certain groups selling clothes, and the operation of an active business there is a difficult area to define; but the basic principle is that the activity should be related to those of the charity and it should not become the vehicle for a substantial commercial business.

I have one more question, Mr. Chairman. I should like to be absolutely clear, further to what the minister just said, that if it were a new business or a new enterprise in which the charity might become involved, it would be subject to review, whereas businesses that are primarily and traditionally associated with those charitable foundations would be accepted by the income tax people as legitimate businesses in furtherance of the cause of that charity.
I am advised that that is the intention of Revenue Canada in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I am fairly certain that this matter has been brought to the attention of the minister, but for the record I should like to express a concern which has been conveyed to a number of members of the House by universities in particular. I do not think I can put the case any better than has the chief financial officer of one of the universities of one of my colleagues. Reference was made in the letter to the green paper on tax treatment of charities which was published in 1975. 1 would like to quote some passages from that letter. One of them reads as follows:
The legislation expected to follow the green paper was given the further purpose of ensuring that the Income Tax Act did "not inhibit charities from carrying on their work in the most effective manner possible".
In further reference to the green paper, the letter indicates that the green paper says this:
"in the fields of education, medicine, scientific research, culture, religion and athletics to name just a few major areas".

Then quoting directly from the letter:
The paper went on to say that the role of charities in these areas was "to fill in gaps of service and financial support where government should not or cannot play a significant part".
This chief financial officer draws the following conclusion from that references to educational institutes that:
-the paper was concerned not with educational institutions as such but with the independent charities which may provide financial assistance to them.
The feeling of this officer is as follows:
-that the legislation was not intended in the first instance to apply to publicly-supported educational institutions.
I would like to quote further from the letter:
The bill would require that we meet a certain prescribed percentage of income disbursement rules. For purposes of these disbursement rules, specific definitions of income are provided. The essence of the income definitions would seem to be that a registered charity would report as income (for purposes of disbursement rules) donations received from sources able to claim deductions for income tax purposes. Donations which would not produce an income tax benefit for the donor, and restricted donations which were to be held for a period of not less than ten years, would by definition be excluded from the calculation of income. The bill also contains a relieving provision that provides for the aggregation of income and disbursements over a period of several years in order to meet disbursement rules.
I do not intend to read the whole letter, but another part of it reads as follows:
If the bill passes as written, we will have to be able to prepare financial statements reporting income and disbursements as defined in the bill. This may not be perceived by others as an especially onerous requirement, but our accounting systems do not allow us to accumulate charitable donations by category of donor and substantial changes would have to be effected in the systems to provide such a capability. We would, I believe, have to develop and implement a charitable donation receipt classification system which would be unrelated to any of our needs or those of our donors.
As I have said, the writer is the chief financial officer of a well known university in Canada. This person also expressed concern about the problems which could arise from the provision in the bill whereby the minister's approval in writing would have to be obtained to accumulate funds for particular purposes. I quote again from the letter as follows:
More analysis on our part as well as additional information from the minister will be required before we can fully assess the effect of this provision but I think it is fair to say that it would probably involve an enormous increase in paper flow between the minister and educational institutions.
As publicly-supported institutions, universities in Canada have for years met all reasonable accountability requirements for the funds entrusted to them. Requiring universities to develop accounting and reporting systems to meet standards intended to control abuses in non-related areas will not help us to carry on our work in "the most effective manner possible". I feel strongly that the application of the proposed controls should be on a more selective basis and that some exempting provision should be made in the bill, either at the minister's discretion, or, perhaps as a specific exemption for universities and other designated educational institutions as defined in section 110(9)(a)( 1) of the Income Tax Act.
In this connection it may be worth noting that those universities outside Canada which are authorized to issue charitable donation receipts acceptable for Canadian income tax purposes would appear to be exempt from the provisions of clause 60 as they are not registered Canadian charitable organizations. The 1975-76 edition of the Income Tax regulations lists 228 such universities. While I certainly would not advocate the extension of clause 60 to these universities, their exclusion from the proposed legislation does represent different treatment from that proposed for Canadian universities and will be more favourable to their costs of fund-raising activities.

Finally, reference is made to the penalty clause which is contained in this bill and the writer concludes the following:
I have not attempted the calculation of this tax as it would relate to (our university) because I cannot conceive of such an application to a Canadian university.
That statement is now on the record. I would like to ask the minister directly what kind of representations he has received in connection with the effect of clause 60, and what changes, if any, are proposed.

Mr. Chairman, I can confirm that the only representation I have received in this regard is from the hon. member's colleague, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, who spoke to me about this on Friday afternoon for the first time and then sent me a letter which included excerpts from the letter the hon. member read into the record and which one can judge by inference was written to the hon. member by somebody at Queen's University.
Although I have not checked with my advisers, I think I would be correct in saying that we did not receive that representation directly from the lady or gentleman of that university, so I cannot be confident at this point whether this question has been discussed previously between the department and the university in question. I go back to the portion of the letter which the hon. member quoted, which reads as follows:
More analysis on our part as well as additional information from the minister will be required before we can fully assess the effect of this provision-
I just indicate that we would be quite prepared to discuss with the representatives of Queen's University or any other university the manner in which they feel the administration of these particular provisions may be onerous to them, and if they would like to do so, I would be pleased to hear from them. I suggest, however, that this is a question of administration. 1 think the initial reaction on the departmental side would be that the difficulties are perhaps overstressed. But I repeat that we would be quite prepared to discuss the application of the law as it may affect the particular group, and to see if amendments might be required in the forthcoming budget.

Just for greater clarification I would like to ask, again, if the minister has received representations from other Canadian universities as to the effect of this clause upon them. At the same time, I would like to ask another question. Is the effect that has been pointed out to the minister what was intended when he made these proposals in the first place?

I am not familiar with any other representations. I would have to have the records checked to see if at any time in the last two years any university has complained in this regard to my officers or to my department. We anticipated that there would have to be some changes in administration involved with the change in the act. That is not an uncommon circumstance. If, indeed, the writer's fears are justified-and I think we could only find that out after, as he or she has said, analysis-then we would be prepared to consider a change in procedures. At the moment we do not think they would be unduly onerous.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few comments on this point. I can readily understand why the minister was moving into the area of, shall we say, high cost-either high cost as to collection, or high cost as to administration-types of charities and into the area where individuals set up charitable foundations, that is, colorable charitable foundations in order to gain for themselves some tax-relieved income.
On the other hand, I feel that in an effort to tackle that type of gain he has armed himself with a high-powered rifle to go after a rabbit. I would say that the problems put forward by Queen's University, as evidenced by the exchange of views between the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra and the minister, are valid for other universities. I would think it is difficult to say to institutions, "Let us see how this goes. In order to comply with this you will have to change your whole accounting system, and then we will look at it." There are areas where the accounting has to be a segregation of income. If a gift is given to a qualified charity within certain limits, that is permitted. But it is already permitted under the act, although that income has to be segregated.
As far as related businesses are concerned, my own University of Alberta took over a student union organization known as HUB, a totally segregated student residence; a business complex for student purposes. Is that to be a related business? What about bookstores, student health services and computing centres? A number of universities have computing centres which have spare time so they provide payroll services, etc., to other organizations. Is this a "related business", and what is to be done with regard to its income?
Section 149.1 (2)(a) of the act gives the minister discretionary power to revoke the registration of a charitable organization that carries on an unrelated business. If any one of these unrelated businesses was unclear and the universities were to engage in that type of operation, does it run the risk of the minister deregistering that university or charity? I think it is quite unfair, unless it is clearly spelled out in the act and not left to determination by the courts or review by the minister. A university does not change its accounting practices as the minister or I might change a jacket.
The other thing that concerns me is in section 149.1(14) and (15). Why are two information returns required? These subclauses read as follows:
(14)	Every registered charity, shall, within three months from the end of each taxation year of the charity, file with the minister both an information return and a public information return for the year, each in prescribed form and containing prescribed information, without notice or demand therefor.
(15)	Notwithstanding section 241 -
Section 241 prohibits the publication of information by any official in a tax department if the information is furnished with respect to a tax return. There is no doubt that the information sought under section 141.1(14) and (15) is respecting income tax. An exception to the confidentiality is being asked for in subsection (15) which reads:

February 7, 1977
Income Tax Act
Notwithstanding section 241, the information contained in a public information return referred to in subsection (14) shall be communicated or otherwise made available to the public by the minister in such manner as he deems appropriate.
Now that shall require a full explanation not only with regard to the universities but with regard to all charities. I ask, very sincerely, why this exception is to be made to the confidentiality of income tax returns. I am not 100 per cent sure, but it would seem to me this is likely the only instance under the Income Tax Act where section 241 is weighted with regard to any particular type of taxpayer. As I say, I am subject to correction on that point, but I am not aware that at any time in the past the minister had the right to communicate to any member of the public the contents of the income tax return of any taxpayer. I would suggest that the burden of proof is on the minister to indicate why that should be done in this particular instance.

The purpose of the requirement is, of course, that the public may know, in a broad category sense, the kind of charitable activity being carried on and the kind of contributions being made. The source of income by broad categories, that is to say, government, corporations, other charities, individuals, etc., the amount expended on charitable activity by broad category-education, research, etc.-gross administrative expenses, including salaries in aggregated form, and basic information of the name, location and function of the charity, is to be in the public information return.
The green discussion paper said that in view of the large tax concessions granted to registered charities, the public is entitled to know with some precision the activities of the charity. The proposal to require disclosure has met a very positive response from most groups, and rules will be incorporated in the legislation. In other words, you have operations being carried out for charitable purposes, ostensibly, being given the benefit of exemption from income tax provisions. In that sense, other taxpayers will have to bear the part of the burden which this activity might otherwise have borne. For this purpose, it seems to me to be reasonable from the public standpoint to have some public disclosure, in the broadest terms, of what the source of funds is and how they are being applied.
Representations have been received to the effect that the public information return should not be so specific as to embarrass the charity or its officers, for example by giving the names of the officers or their home telephone numbers where they could be subject to contact, or the names of the beneficiaries of grants, and an information circular will be issued by Revenue Canada to make this clear. The basic purpose, however, is that when you have an organization being run for the public benefit, the public should be entitled to know, in the broadest categories, as to the purpose, the source of funds, how they are applied and what the administrative expenses are. Hence, the disclosure formula.

With regard to the carrying on of a business, it ought to be remembered that under the existing provisions of the Income Tax Act no business can be carried on by a charity. Therefore, in that sense the proposed amendment is of a relieving category.
The hon. member referred to activities at a university, for example, the provision of student accommodation, food and computer services for the benefit of students. Clearly, in those circumstances those activities would be related services and I would anticipate no difficulty at all. If a university at a certain point develops a computer service, say, to the point where it is engaging in a substantial commercial business, a business substantially more commercial than that of supplying a service to its own students, at that particular point Revenue Canada may indeed have to consider the status of that particular operation. In general, those services which are made available to the student body or for the purposes of the educational operation are clearly related businesses and would be so considered and permitted under the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Chairman, I take it that the only authority the minister invoked today was based on the government's own green paper. I am referring to the intentions which it published in the green paper. Am I correct in suggesting that that is the sole, shall we say, criterion or authority on which it bases its conclusions as expressed in the bill?
Mr. Chairman, I am not sure what the hon. member means by "the only authority." Of course, the question was much canvassed in the green paper.
That was the government's green paper.

The government's green paper, which was much canvassed, as I remarked. The proposal received substantial support from those who responded to that paper. With regard to this point and the point concerning universities generally, the matter has been out in the forum of public discussion for close to two years. I think it is fair to say that there has been substantial agreement on the part of those responsible for operating charitable organizations in Canada with the proposals made. Although the green paper may have been the government's own green paper, it seems to have received substantial support from those most affected by it.
Silence is not always golden.

Mr. Chairman, may I raise a question concerning charities which may have gone into business and which generate a substantial part of their moneys with business? Am I to take it that the provision mentioned would affect, say, neighbourhood services and other organizations in related fields, organizations which sell to the public and whose revenue derived from that operation is used for the purposes of charity? Am I correct in assuming that no matter how much
February 7, 1977

of the income is derived from such operation, that operation will still be considered as a charity?

Exactly, Mr. Chairman. The operation, for example, of the Ottawa Neighbourhood Services, which sells clothing and furniture and, in my own city, of the Crippled Civilians, would be exactly the kind of related business which we have in mind.
Mr. Chairman, is it the government's intention to exempt these organizations from the charities act, or to bring them under it?

The intention was to make it clear that if a charitable organization carried on this particular line of business, it would not cease to lose its category as a charity so as to lose exemption from income tax.

Mr. Chairman, I see by the clock that but two or three minutes remain for discussing this important clause: discussion is to cease under the iniquitous closure rule imposed on us by the government. We are dealing here with a clause that has to do with the surtax which people earning over $30,000 a year were paying. This provision was introduced in an attempt to make the tax system fair and to complement the work of the Anti-Inflation Board which limited the maximum increases in earnings of ordinary Canadians to $2,400 a year. In the previous budget, the Minister of Finance admitted that it is difficult to keep track of professional incomes which are affected by dividends and other kinds of profit-sharing plans. He therefore wanted to impose a surtax on taxable income over $8,000 to make sure that professionals and other upper income Canadians bear their fair share of the burden of the government's war on inflation.
Income Tax Act
We find from an examination of Anti-Inflation Board reports that professionals have exceeded the $2,400 maximum, averaging increases of some $4,900 a year. What is more, the present provision in the bill will govern only the surtax for the year 1976: it does not extend it to the year 1977. To that the New Democratic Party seriously objects. Mr. Speaker, it is sometimes very revealing and constructive to have debates such as we have had on Bill C-22. Members have revealed their true thoughts about particular situations or issues. One such situation prevented itself last Thursday. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), in the debate on childcare deductions, stated that the working spouse is more of a social phenomenon than an economic necessity. He cited a letter which stated that women should stay at home and look after their children, and that children who go through day care centres are almost social monsters. He seemed critical of families where both husbands and wives work and hence benefit from child care deductions, whereas families where the wives do not work receive no benefit. The hon. member went further, calling for joint income tax returns to be filed by a family group. I received a letter from a constituent, a woman. She made some points which the hon. member for Edmonton West failed to take into consideration. I quote from the letter:
Dear John:
I am concerned about the narrow minded opinions that many of the politicians in the Conservative party have with respect to women's rights.
The working woman is not a social phenomenon.
February 7, 1977

The hon. member stood up last Thursday and said that. All the women on the government benches just sat there and took it. This woman went on in her letter:
For most women a job is a necessity rather than a pastime.
She quoted Sylvia Gelber, a consultant to the federal Department of Labour. This is what Ms. Gelber found:
Adding up the estimated 331,434 women who are the sole support of their families, 925,000 single working women and an estimated 678,035 working wives whose husbands have a median income of $6,454 a year, it is safe to assume that most women work because of economic need.
The letter continues:
On top of that how can anyone assume that the man and not the woman is working for economic necessity. In the case where both the husband and the wife are working, has anyone stopped to ask whether the man is working because he wants to and not because he has to. If these politicians would ask themselves that question they would probably come to the conclusion that society does not question a man's decision to work. But a woman is expected to play the role of housewife and mother and the minute she diverges from that role she is viewed as a social phenomenon, a social anomaly.
This is the typical attitude of the Conservative party. They expect women and other minority groups to behave in a certain manner which is consistent with their stereotypic vision of society.
I am a woman and also a human being. I am not an appendage of my husband and have the right to decide whether I want to work outside the home. Regardless of my husband's salary level, society has no right to impose a certain role on me. The right to decide whether to work in the home or to pursue a career is a matter of individual choice and human rights.
Judy Wasylycia'leis.
I should give the name of the constituent: it is Judy Wasylycia'leis. All I can say to that is "Amen". I wish the Tories would not be so phony on the hustings, representing themselves as the friend of women, the friend of youth, the friend of the unemployed, the friend of labour, the friend of the working class. Then they have the other group, the Bay Street boys. They are their biggest friends and allies. Here is where we see the great allies come together.
When we started the debate on Bill C-22 we tried to point out how regressive this income tax structure is. We watched the Tories defend the legislation. They represent one element in Canadian society-those who have made it. The Tories want to protect the status quo. Bill C-22 is being introduced at a time when study after study is showing that the economic inequality gap in Canada is growing wider. Contrary to Liberal mythology, there is no doubt that the rich are getting richer while the poor are getting poorer. The distribution of wealth in Canada is completely unfair, and we have put together the evidence to support this assertion. The report recently released by the Economic Council is a sad commentary on the existing state of affairs. In 1965 the top one-fifth of the population with an average income of $12,000 a year was getting nine times as much as the average for the bottom fifth's $1,300. Last year, the top group received $29,000, about 11 times as much as the $2,600 in the lowest income group.
Professor Irwin Gillespie of Carleton University did a major study on income distribution in Canada. He is convinced that anyone who believes Canadian society is becoming more egalitarian is living in a dream world. The distribution of

money income did not change significantly between 1951 and 1974: the poorest one-fifth had 4.4 per cent in 1951, and 4 per cent in 1974; the richest one-fifth had 42.8 per cent of money income in 1951, and 42.4 per cent in 1974. According to the Senate Committee on Poverty, 27 per cent of Canadian households were under the poverty line in 1973. A more moderate figure of 23 per cent was reported by the Council on Social Development. This means that about one person in four, in one of the richest countries in the world, can be described as poor.
Another revealing study is by Professor N. H. Chi, also of Carleton University. He documents the statement that the gap between the rich and the poor is growing and that this inequality means dire consequences for the stability of Canadian society. I quote from this study:
It is true that economic progress has brought an increase in real per capita income which doubled in the years between 1951 and 1971. However, during the same period, "progress" brought a remarkable and disturbing increase in the level of inequality of income. Except for the years 1951-57, the gap between rich and poor grew wider in the form of a parabolic curve.
Professor Chi clearly documents the relationship between inequality and social problems in Canada. In the years between 1951 and 1971, the rising level of inequality in the distribution of income coincided with a pattern of growing labour unrest which took the form of strikes and lock-outs. It seems that the frustrations from working hard but not getting ahead can also account for the increasing crime rate. Inequality also results in psychological and emotional stress. It is not surprising, therefore, that Professor Chi should have found that mental illness, alcoholism and suicide rates have risen drastically since 1951 and followed the curve of increasing inequality.
The Liberal government says it is concerned about income distribution. But if it is interested, if it is so concerned, why has nothing been done during the nine years during which the Liberals have been in power? Why has it chosen to introduce Bill C-22 which makes the tax system even more regressive than it is now? It can only mean one thing: the Liberal government wants to hold inequality steady, or maybe increase it. Once more the Trudeau administration is insisting that the income tax system, the most logical and efficient instrument for income redistribution, must not be disturbed. Instead of using the tax system to distribute wealth more equitably, the government is allowing the affluent to shelter their incomes with the encouragement of the Income Tax Act. Just as Leonard Shifrin stated on December 29, 1976, in the Ottawa Citizen:
This government never ceases to amaze me. Every time I become convinced that it has exhausted all possible means of increasing the maldistribution of income in this country, it confounds me with yet another breathtaking initiative.
While mouthing platitudes about equality and income redistribution, the government is attempting to get away with an increasing number of tax breaks for the rich. It is clear the rich do not have to apply for welfare: they get it free from the Liberals. It is also, clear, from reading Bill C-22, that the true Liberal philosophy goes further than: if you work hard, you

The government's attitude toward taxation is essentially one of making tax-dodging legal. This favours the erosion of the progressive taxation system which encourages those who have the ability to pay to take steps, legally, to minimize their tax contribution. It is this attitude which is largely responsible for the appearance of articles such as that which was published in the Citizen on December 20, 1976. The author is Paul Dioguardi-I presume he is an economist-who wrote:
As year-end draws closer, it is time once again to consider ways of minimizing or deferring taxes. Happily, this chore has been made a little easier by a tax bulletin put out by Coopers and Lybrand, chartered accountants. It has touched on some of the important points to be considered in year-end tax planning.
I always thought, Mr. Speaker, that the point of this whole income tax exercise was to determine what it cost to run this country and then to set about collecting taxes from the people, according to their ability to pay, so as to cover the cost of those programs and services. But here we see that anyone engaged in a banking or accountancy business of some kind is given advice about the best way of avoiding the payment of taxes on income. If all of us did that, how would we get the money to run the country and pay for the present level of programs and services?
It seems to me there is only one group which can benefit from that kind of tax-dodging: it is not the working poor; it has to be those who take a lot out of the economy. May I quote now from an article which appeared in the Financial Post of December 4 under the heading, "Time running out fast if you want to declare a tax loss this year." This article, by Beatrice Riddell, stated:
Time is fast running out for those who would like to get on with certain tax planning schemes which may reduce or defer 1976 income.
The game of tax-dodging is inherent in the system which creates numerous exemptions and deductions which are beneficial largely to high income earners. The income tax legislation already contains 17 subsidies which cost Canadians approximately $6.4 billion in 1974. The National Council of Welfare calculates that this $6.4 billion could have been used to provide every family in Canada with an extra $100 a month for food and clothing. Instead, it was used to improve the position of the well-off, while the poor whose incomes were below the tax threshold received no benefit at all. Imagine a government expenditure program which gave ten times as much to those with incomes over $25,000 than it did to those with incomes less than $5,000!
A government which is the least bit concerned would have spent this money equally on all sectors. I know that we cannot expect this government to transfer more money to the poor than to the rich, because they are playing a game with the Tories, trying to get the electoral support of people in the upper income brackets. They are trying to prove how much more of a friend to the wealthy they are than the Tories. This is the kind of political game that is being played-a very cynical, hypocritical one.

It has been clearly documented that deductions stand the "ability to pay" principle on its head, and that tax credits in fixed amounts, when justified for social reasons, constitute a more equitable distribution of government expenditures. This government has never accepted that principle. I quote from the report entitled "The hidden welfare system":
When a deduction is offered instead of a credit, it means the government has chosen to do in a hidden fashion what it would never do openly-grant bigger subsidies to those of high incomes than to those with low incomes.
In full knowledge of this-not unknowingly, but in full knowledge-this government has chosen, through Bill C-22, to further increase the number of tax deductions and deferrals, which can only add to the regressivity of the way Canadians pay their income taxes. Amazingly, it has increased deductions for registered pension plans, registered retirement savings plans, child care and disability allowances.
And who benefits?

The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie asks, who benefits? We know who benefits. We have been through this bill clause by clause and we have tried to amass the facts and to present the picture of who actually benefits from Bill C-22. Contrary to what the Minister of Finance said last Monday, we in this party who have tried to examine this bill in detail are not ill-advised, as he suggested we are. Even if the minister could prove that deductions through pension plans benefit the middle income taxpayers, he has not shown how such plans will benefit the poor who have no hope of saving money for retirement.
The minister has not proven to us how the poor people are going to benefit by increasing the tax free amounts that are being invested in registered retirement savings plans. He also ignores the fact that the RRSP is not being used primarily as a means of saving for retirement; rather, the RRSP is being used by middle and high income earners as a means of escaping taxes owed. As Mr. Dioguardi stated in his column in the Citizen of January 31 last:
It is high time taxpayers considered pursuing the noble goal of wresting a few dollars from the tax collector's greedy grasp. The most straightforward method to achieve this goal involves the tried and true registered retirement savings plan.
Mr. Speaker, isn't that something? Even the hon. member for Edmonton West has got to admit that is pretty blatant.
Your view is that they are designed to be taxed.

A progressive tax system should be designed so that every man pays his fair share of taxes on what he earns. It should not be designed so that a man can manipulate the tax system and write things off, because poor people cannot take advantage of that. That has not got through his thick skull yet. That is the problem with you Tories. It takes a long time for any idea to sink through your thick skulls. As my mother used to say, you have got to be a numbskull. I just do not understand it, Mr. Speaker. Surely every member of the House can understand that except the hon. member for
February 7, 1977

Edmonton West. We have told them once, if we have told them a thousand times.
He is not alone; there are a few others like him.

But they always run him up to the front to make a speech to defend the "haves" in this country. Then they get someone from Atlantic Canada to make a speech on behalf of the "have-nots", so they can suck and blow at the same time. They do that consistently in this House. They did it when we were debating the unemployment insurance bill when it was before the House. They have done that all down the line.
Let us look at three examples which show how the RRSP is used as a means of tax-dodging. I would like the hon. member for Edmonton West to tell the House how poor people earning under $10,000 a year can take advantage of these tax dodges. The first way of using an RRSP as a tax dodge is the spousal RRSP, which can be used to split income. The husband who is in a high income range can use the RRSP to divert funds to his wife, who will pay tax at a lower rate when the funds are repatriated.
Secondly, an RRSP can be used effectively to convert part of a taxpayer's home mortgage interest expense into tax deductible interest. These are tax dodges, Mr. Speaker, and surely that is not what an RRSP was set up to be. Surely it was set up so people can save, and then when they retire get an income. Is the purpose of an RRSP that it be used as a tax dodge? If so, it is not fair. There is not a Tory or a Liberal in the House who can stand up and tell me point-blank that it is fair. It is lousy, and they ought to be ashamed of themselves.
But that can be done even by a man earning $6,000.
A lot of guys who are earning $6,000 can go to the bank and borrow $2,000. Bill C-16 has to do with giving low income earners an opportunity to get credit when they need it.
There are a lot more honest people earning $6,000 than you would admit.

Thirdly, an individual who invests in an RRSP can defer the tax on the accumulated earnings of his annuity plan while deducting the interest cost of the money borrowed to invest in the annuity. That is a neat dodge. I suppose that anyone earning less than $10,000 can walk into his friendly bank manager's office and borrow $2,500. But, by golly, his wife cannot go down to the bank and do that because sometimes banks do not recognize that a wife can be a wage earner in her own right, and they may refuse to grant her a loan or they only consider 50 per cent of her salary for loan purposes. That is discriminatory. I do not hear the great defender of the banking system talking about such discriminatory aspects, yet he has the gall to stand in this House and declare that the working woman is a social phenomenon. I think working Tories are a social phenomenon.

There are more working Tories than there are working NDP'ers.
If you want to make a speech, go and sit in your own seat.
We are not as sanctimonious as you are.

I know that. Another example of the regressive nature of this bill is to be found in clause 21 which increases deductions for child care expenses from $500 to $1,000 per child, and the per family maximum from $2,000 to $4,000. The National Council of Welfare has illustrated how the tax saving from this deduction is substantially more beneficial to the wealthy than to the lower income groups. At the $10,000 level, such a $1,000 deduction would be worth $210, while in the $50,000 plus category it is worth $410. Last Monday, the Minister of Finance claimed that the quarter of a million of Canadians who claimed child care allowance stand to benefit from the increase. I am afraid that the minister misses the point completely and this type of deduction maintains constant inequality. The greater the deduction, the greater the inequality. Members on the government benches over there seem to operate on the principle that all persons are equal, except that some are more equal than others.
Not only does this bill deliberately improve the tax position of the middle and upper income earners; it does absolutely nothing to plug the existing loopholes which turn the ability to pay principle upside down. It does nothing to change the fact that in 1974 deletions from the accounts of income tax revenue that could not be collected because the taxpayers were no longer resident in Canada amounted to $850,000 owed by 161 taxpayers. Why are the names of those tax dodgers not published? What effort is the Department of National Revenue making to collect the money that these people owe the people of Canada?
It does nothing to change the fact that in 1974, 252 persons who made over $50,000 paid no tax at all, and 17 of them had incomes of over $200,000. These are the kind of people for whom the frontbench Tories stand up all the time. We saw one standing up for John Doyle-a nice working-class Canadian! That is the kind of defence they put up. When we defend people in the House, I can assure you we do not defend people such as John Doyle, or Bell Canada; we talk about working-class Canadians.
This bill does nothing to change the fact that professionals who want to avoid paying taxes set up dummy companies since small businesses pay taxes at a lower rate compared with marginal rates in the personal income tax system. Bill C-22 does nothing to change the fact that interest costs on money borrowed for the purpose of investing in something that may ultimately earn income for the taxpayer are deductible for the year in which the expense is incurred. We can look at the example which was provided by that Liberal in Manitoba whom everyone knows: they call him Dizzy Asper.

Oh, oh!

If any hon. member wishes to make a speech, I will listen to him. If he does not have the courage to stand up and make a speech, let him go behind the curtains and sip his tea. Here is an example of the way in which Mr. Asper suggests things should be done. He says:
Jones earns $100,000 a year and pays $50,000 in tax.
I will need the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) to help me with this one. It goes on to read:
He borrows $1 million on January 1 at 10 per cent interest and secures the loan by a stock portfolio of $1 million in cost, which he bought with the bank loan. On December 31 of that year he has incurred an interest cost of $100,000 which he offsets against his $1,000,000 income-
There it is. Voila, says Mr. Asper, no tax! At least we know that the man who borrowed $1 million from Obront paid a fair interest on it: he borrowed $1 million and paid $ 1V2 million in interest. That is the kind of interest I am prepared to accept.
Finally, this bill does nothing to stop income-splitting or loans made by a husband to a spouse, or a father to his children, on an interest-free basis. The consequences of this are best revealed by another piece of advice from Mr. Asper which appeared in the Globe and Mail. This guy Asper is a fount of information on tax-dodging.
He is a Liberal.

His buddy wrote it. He was probably consulted. Here is his suggestion:
The father who is in the 60 per cent tax bracket and has a wife and three children (it gets even more exciting when there are grandchildren) can lend his brood $400,000, interest-free, which they invest in 10 per cent preferred shares. Assuming they have no other income, the $40,000 they collectively receive in dividends will bear no tax because of the Canadian dividend tax credit system.
The only little touch in that is that you must have $400,000 to lend. You can walk to a bank and get a $400,000 credit. I am sure that the miners in Nickel Belt and the steelworkers in Sault Ste. Marie can walk to the Imperial Bank or to the Royal Bank of Canada and say, "Boys, I want to borrow 400,000 bucks"! This is the way in which the experts and the Liberals view the tax system. This is not a method of paying one's fair share to support the country and to support the programs of the country. They use the tax system to dodge taxes.
May I call it, five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME PLAN
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to establish a guaranteed annual income plan, which should be designed to encourage any able-bodied person to work, in order to correct the social injustices resulting from existing legislation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my motion No. 20 was allowed to stand last Monday at the request of the government on account of a storm in my riding. The same thing is happening today to a representative from Nova Scotia. Therefore, it is through an arrangement made by two parliamentarians that the motion standing in my name is called at this time.
I do not have to go over the motion just read by the Speaker because every member in this House knows about it. However, for the benefit of Canadian citizens as a whole, I must say first of all that I myself could have introduced such a piece of legislation to this effect. But, because of current procedures in the House of Commons, an hon. member is not allowed to introduce a bill involving expenditures of taxpayers' money. That privilege is now granted the ministers of the Crown alone, though they must be, first and foremost, members of the House of Commons. That is why an hon. member who is not a minister, regardless of whether he belongs to the majority party or even the Liberal party, now in power, does not have the privilege of introducing a bill involving the expenditure of money. That rule is a very old British tradition. However, it should be changed to meet the needs of Canadian aspirations in 1977.
To my mind, true democracy should differ from what we have known to date. As parliament is the general assembly of all the representatives of the Canadian people, I cannot see why that assembly should not be, in fact, the supreme authority in the land. The supreme will of the people could then be executed by the executive council known as the council or the cabinet of ministers presided over by the Prime Minister, and as such, designated by the representatives of the party in the majority.
Mr. Speaker, to be efficient and beneficial to all Canadian citizens, the economic system of a country such as ours should be able to ensure each and everyone a decent subsistence. For that, it must be constituted properly and only on that condition will it achieve its end, namely enable each and everyone to meet his needs. To achieve that end, the Social Credit Party of Canada has suggested one means: the distribution, periodically, of a monthly dividend to all Canadians; in other words, giving each citizen in the country the benefit of a discount equal to the GNP surplus after the deduction of public expenditures for the various public services given to the citizens by the state.
Private Members' Motions
The surplus should be refunded to the public either as a rebate such as in a co-operative or as dividends in a capital stock company or as guaranteed annual income to each citizen. It does not matter, the words or names are not important, but the results obtained and enjoyed by each Canadian are, whatever may be his age, status, social position.
When Mr. Douglas, the author of the social credit philosophy submitted that formula, the economists were laughing at him since they considered his policy utopian, that is an ideology which is logical but impracticable in the orthodox financial conditions under which we are living.
Now, since 1935 while that man was suggesting that citizens of a community such as Canada should enjoy social benefits as a cultural heritage, namely old age security pension, family allowances, national dividend, compensated discount, we have accomplished much progress and members of parliament and society itself are more than ever supporting the principle.
I remember reading over and over again the encyclics of Popes Leo XIII and Pius XI on the social and economic problems of the years 1891 to 1931 and which contained direct recommendations to governments for implementing policies devised to help workers and small farmers and earners, such as family allowances and a guaranteed family income.
I also remember this favorite phrase of our labour leaders: equal pay for equal work, but to everyone according to his needs. That created astonishment at first, but as time elapsed, the idea made its way, so that it was finally accepted that women were entitled to equal pay and to a decent family income. That is why the legislation authorizing the payment of family allowances was finally passed by the Canadian parliament.
May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that from 1930 to 1945, I was, among many others, an advocate of the family allowances policy. With astonishing impudence, egotistical and blind opponents despised us as Utopians because we believed that each family was entitled to an income proportionate to its needs and that the state had to pay family allowances to families according to the number of children and the economic wealth of the country. We were then charged with being communists. Yet God knows we are not champions of Karl Marx's doctrine, but supporters of free enterprise. That does not mean we are in favour of the capitalist philosophy, which would allow the powerful under the present capitalist system to realize excessive profits by every means, even by exploiting the poor because they are defenceless.
We believe a responsible government's role is to monitor the development of economic activities and prevent the powerful from taking unfair advantage of the underprivileged as it is unfortunately too often the case today. It is not the capitalist system which is bad per se, but rather the excesses of capitalism. That is why we must open our eyes to the truth, however hard and bitter it may be. The capitalist system will be reformed by men of order, or it will be destroyed by the others.
