In my opinion, it will not remain as it is under its present form, which is not totally bad, but its operation will. We have all if not chosen at least accepted to live within a society because we saw that it was more advantageous to live so and that under this formula we could meet our needs more efficiently. Nevertheless, this society life offers in itself many advantages, which I do not have time to list, but anyone can discover them by thinking a little.
However, despite all the advantages it offers, this life within a society also means that each citizen incurs obligations which he must accept and meet: there could be no rights without obligations. This is, in my opinion, the true democracy. This being said, it does not mean that the state does not have duties towards the community. Its duty is to administer the community wealth to the advantage of everybody and make sure that human capital and money capital get their share from this association but that the latter does not exploit human capital and work capital, as it is unfortunately the case too often.
Second, taking into consideration the performance and the effectiveness of the combined efforts of human capital with money capital, the state must from year to year make a compilation and then ensure that human capital and money capital get their share without injustice for the other form of capital that is human capital. The share accruing to human capital will be distributed in the form of guaranteed annual income and salaries while the share accruing to money capital will be distributed during the fiscal year in the form of profits and dividends at the end of the business fiscal year.
Now, if you examine the rather constant increase in gross national output you find that human capital did not get its share regularly, hence the blatant social injustices which gnaw at society. That is why there is an immediate need to introduce an annual guaranteed income plan which first would provide people 60 years of age or over as well as widows and handicapped people with an income allowing everyone of those people to meet their needs and then those of the Canadian society as a whole.
As of April 1, 1976, Canada spent nearly $4 billion to provide some form of annual income to people 60 years of age or over. In addition, at the same date, Canada spent $1,957 million on family allowances for 7,900,000 children between the ages of 0 to 18. So we still have to make all other people between the ages of 18 and 59 eligible for a guaranteed annual income, as follows: 3 million people between the ages of 19 to 25; 4,700,000 people between the ages of 26 to 40; 2,547,000 people between the ages of 41 to 50; as well as 1,960,000 people between the ages of 51 to 59. There are 6,154,700 males, and 6,095,200 females, for a total of 12,249,900 people-a little more than half the population of this country.
We must therefore conclude that this group is responsible for the major part of economic activities and that the same goes for income tax, which is the main source of revenue for the state. This group of citizens is entitled to its share, and the state must recognize this by establishing a guaranteed annual income plan such as we have been promoting for many years

under the honest and thoughtful direction of our lamented leader who was also a great Canadian, Real Caouette, whose premature death I and many other Canadians deplore. Mr. Speaker, this political leader spent a large portion of his life promoting an economic and monetary reform based on the philosophy of Major Douglas aimed at establishing an economic system which would be fairer to all Canadians, whatever their language and religion. Of course, people who have wanted to preserve a status quo to make a profit have ridiculed the theories of Mr. Douglas, even though they were accepted by many serious people, like Mr. Aberhart, Alberta premier for many years, Mr. Bennett, from British Columbia, Mr. Goldsborough, from the House of Representatives of the United States, and Mr. Real Caouette and his colleagues in the Canadian parliament.
Mr. Real Caouette very often stated in this parliament his views about including in our statutes this formula of a guaranteed annual income so as to provide everyone with a sufficient income. I am certain that this formula will one day be included in the statutes of Canada, but the longer this is postponed, the more serious our problems will become and the greater the inequities of the system will be.
It is time to act. To make a choice is evidence of maturity, like the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in Quebec City on January 28, 1977. This is what Mr. Real Caouette did, this is what thousands of Canadians have done, this is what my colleagues and I have done when we chose a socially distributed credit system instead of the credit-debt system that we have been using since the beginning of our Confederation, on July 1, 1867, and which no longer meets the needs of today.
At that time, the debt of Canada was $79 million, but it is now $64 billion. This choice of the credit debt system is impoverishing us and forcing us to pay $15 million a day in interest when we could do something else without printing dollar bills, like the Prime Minister said, but by taking into account the efficiency and production of all Canadians, like Social Crediters suggest, and by making the accounting mechanism of the Bank of Canada follow. We, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, propose a change in our financial system. Why? Because we sincerely believe that the present system no longer meets our needs.
In a democracy, it is normal to want to change the tools which no longer correspond to today's realities. We are conscious of these realities and this is why we insist on asking for a change in the financial system so as to establish in the near future a guaranteed annual income system, based on the collective performance rather than the debts of Canadians.
A few years ago, many people in important positions and otherwise mocked the economic and monetary reform suggestions of Mr. Real Caouette and the Social Party of Canada, but today, all honest and serious politicians realize that the guaranteed annual income formula is very valuable and should be implemented if we really want to control misery and settle the two problems of inflation and unemployment. Very knowledgeable people, Mr. Speaker, consider a guaranteed annual

income program as the first step towards a kind of family income, an equitable redistribution of the national wealth in this country.
It is important that we pass as soon as possible a bill designed to fill the gap between the lower and upper income brackets in this country. I believe it is most urgent and pressing that the level of guaranteed income be high enough to ensure a decent life and a full involvement in Canadian society. Sharing of the national wealth of Canada is ill-organized at present and maintains many of our fellow citizens in misery. This situation should be of serious concern to all those who take some interest in the future of our country.
The guaranteed annual income constitutes an income supplement which benefits poor workers, small farmers, small fishermen, non-organized as well as union workers, employees on a temporary or seasonal job, and even more like widows who have not yet reached the age of 60. subsubtopic: SUGGESTED LEGISLATION TO ESTABLISH GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on the motion of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) concerning a guaranteed annual income plan. I am sure hon. members on all sides of the House highly esteem the hon. member for the sincerity with which he has brought forward his motion and spoken today. Since I have been a member of this House I have heard the hon. member more than once raise this issue and speak in support of it forcefully and strongly. I think most members of the House, myself included, support the hon. member to some degree when he says that a guaranteed annual income is important; but it is important to make sure that it will provide an incentive to work, not a disincentive to work. That concept, I think, will find general support on both sides of the House.
As the hon. member said, the government recognizes the importance of this general area and has committed itself to a course of action which essentially bears on the matters the hon. member raised in his motion. As hon. members know, early in 1973 the government initiated action for meeting objectives set out in the motion raised this afternoon. At that time, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) tabled in this House a working paper on social security in Canada and, as well, chaired a joint federal-provincial social security review. During the course of that review many major initiatives were taken which have contributed greatly to the attainment of the type of income security system which presumably is the fundamental objective for Canadians of the motion of the hon. member for Bellechasse.
During the course of the review, a wide range of improvement to the over-all income security system for Canadians was put into effect. In addition, the social security system also saw the emergence of a system of income support and supplementation which would replace Canada's'current welfare system. The Minister of National Health and Welfare advanced these proposals, which constituted a form of guaranteed annual income system, to his provincial colleagues one year ago-last February.
The reform of Canada's welfare system, a reform which would be effected by the implementation of these proposals, conforms precisely to the objective as set forth in the motion of the hon. member who spoke so well this afternoon. In his motion, the hon. member for Bellechasse called our attention to the necessity of ensuring that any guaranteed income system provides strong incentives for productivity and self-reli-

February 7, 1977
Private Members' Motions
ance of those who can work. That same concern was voiced as a matter of top priority throughout the course of the social security review. Indeed, the first proposal of the working paper on social security stated:
-the income security system should remove any disincentives which may exist to discourage people who are on social assistance from taking advantage of the training and employment opportunities available to them, and thus from becoming wholly self-dependent. It should also take care to eliminate any incentive which may now exist for people to shift from employment to social assistance, by reason of the higher benefits which might thus be obtained.
I subscribe strongly to the views I have just quoted. If the hon. member will read my speech delivered in the throne speech debate, he will note that I spoke at length about productivity and the need to make sure that our social security system in Canada helps people to enter and remain in the work force and be useful citizens, and that it should not encourage them to go on welfare or leave the work force since any such encouragement in the long run would not be of service to our people.
The hon. member raised certain of the concerns which were raised in the social security review. It is true that our current welfare system provides some Canadians with disincentives to work which are very real. As a member of parliament, I have talked to many people who have voiced such concerns. Although it is true that there are disincentives in the system, 1 would argue that they are not as widespread as many people seem to think. On the other hand, we would be wrong to contend that there are no disincentives in the system. For many persons currently on provincial social assistance there are powerful financial disincentives associated with return to employment. In some instances, for every dollar they earn they lose a dollar of social assistance; that is, they face a marginal tax rate of 100 per cent on their earnings.
If other Canadians were to face the same tax rate, they would not remain silent. I am sure that the effectiveness of this disincentive needs no further elaboration. Indeed, when compulsory deductions and work-related expenses are taken into account the recipient may face the unappealing prospect of exchanging $1 of social assistance for 80 cents or 90 cents of take-home pay. In some cases, accepting even part-time employment can lead to total loss of benefits. In addition, return to employment can mean the loss of a whole array of benefits in kind, such as dental care and subsidized housing. From a financial point of view at least there is real substance to the complaint that some people are better off on welfare than they are working. I am sure all members of the House will agree that this is wrong.
These financial disincentives are often reinforced by failure at the administrative level to assist the recipients to translate into reality the desire to return to employment. There is no question that the vast majority of people on welfare have special problems in terms of finding and keeping jobs. Often many of them are marginally attached to the work force. Quite often these people have had serious industrial accidents. Perhaps they have low qualifications for jobs that have an increased technology factor. Often the resources made available for equipping these people to overcome these problems are

virtually non-existent. I wish to depart for a moment to speak about one of the major concerns I have in this area.
I understand all provinces have some form of workmen's compensation. This is an area that should be studied. Many of my constituents who have been injured have come to seek my assistance. They have had a period of time on workmen's compensation benefits. They have received some therapy in an attempt to restore them to the work force. However, often the part of a person that is most seriously damaged is the emotional system. A person whose hand has been crippled may still have some use of it, but he cannot do his job as well as he could previously. It therefore becomes difficult to be at ease in his former work situation.
Many of these people become unemployed and subsequently look for other work. Because of some degree of disability they may find it very difficult to find an attachment to the work force. Ultimately they end up on social security, welfare, if you want to use that term, municipally administered. That is how they sustain themselves and quite often their families. What we need is an intermediate step that would assist these people to move back into the work force.
People coming off workmen's compensation benefits who cannot attach themselves to the work force are often faced with a situation that seems to be more prevalent than many of us would like to admit. They may have worked for an employer who has very little patience with people who have physical disabilities caused by an injury in their own plants and so they are subsequently laid off. I really have difficulty understanding the consciences of employers who do that. It happens more often than any of us would care to admit.
I feel very strongly about these people. Even though they were once productive, loyal employees, they end up in a welfare situation. Once they have this emotional problem, it is very difficult to get them back into the work force. It should be pointed out that many of them would actually lose money by returning to work because they cannot get back their old jobs, or one that pays at a level high enough to make it worth their while. We set up a whole syndrome for people to become dependent on these benefits. The situation talked about in the review of gradually working back into the work force and being allowed to keep many of the benefits would be very desirable.
I had not intended to digress in this manner, but in the past two or three weeks I have had a number of representations from constituents who have had industrial accidents. They are deemed to be physically well by those who are trying to rehabilitate them. However, because of emotional damage they have great difficulty returning to work and coping with the noise, emotion, and stress put on them by work with which they were originally quite able to cope. Often this results in a conflict between that type of person and his employer, and his employment is terminated. Such a person finds himself in the position of having somewhat of a physical disability and a very large emotional disability as the result of not having a job. It is
February 7, 1977

soul destroying to watch these people lose their self-esteem and respect.
In terms of the motion put forward by the hon. member and the review of the social assistance program, we want to ensure that we have some means of helping these people who are affected by the types of problems about which I have been talking. There are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are clinging to their independence despite the fact that, in financial terms at least, they would be better off on welfare. These are the working poor. They want to work, work hard, but are rewarded very little for doing so.
Many of the people I was talking about a moment ago have some form of disability, either physical or emotional, as a result of an industrial accident. Only a small proportion of them have any contact with the world of welfare. Most of them do not. That is a testimony to the value Canadians put on self-reliance and the work ethic.
We often hear that no one wants to work any more. Quite a lot is made of that when criticism is made of social programs we have to help people. I take issue with that.
I represent a constituency that probably has one of the highest average incomes in all of Canada. However, there are thousands of people in my constituency, and I am sure in the constituencies of almost every member, who are not at the high end of the income scale. These people want very much to work. However, because of their qualifications and how life unfolded for them, they do not receive a very high financial return for their endeavours. In fact many of them, with technology changing in the work force as much as it is, find themselves in a very difficult position. Rather than forcing these people out of the work force, there ought to be some kind of assistance for them. Programs must be organized to help these people supplement their income. It must be done in a way that ensures these people stay in the work force in the meantime.
A good many of these people have families, perhaps families that are larger in number than those of higher income people. Most of them have paying jobs year round, but their income is inadequate relative to their responsibilities. Other members of the family, other than the principal wage earner, have to go into the work force just to make sure the family unit can survive. I note that a typical family of four in this group would earn between $4,000 and $8,000 a year.
Removing the inequities that exist between these people and those currently on welfare is essential. We must reinforce their self-reliance and provide incentives that reward them rather than create disincentives further inducing them to withdraw from the labour force.
The hon. member's motion implies there are other problems which plague Canada's welfare system. There exists currently a bewildering array of federal, provincial, and municipal programs with related objectives in the area of income maintenance. Not only do the provisions in terms of benefits, conditions of eligibility and so on vary widely, but there is no consistency from one program to the next even on such basic
Private Members' Motions
terms of reference as the definition of income and the definition of a family unit.
Anyone who doubts that statement need only spend sometime in a constituency office trying to help those who come for advice and for whatever assistance their MP can give. They are really bewildered as to who is responsible for which program. Many people are of the opinion that a municipal welfare program is a program of the federal government and administered by it.
Even with regard to old age security, in terms of understanding the old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement and, in the province of Ontario, the Gains program, there is very great difficulty. This has to be sincerely studied. The federal proposals for income support and supplementation came to grips squarely with these problems. Unlike the current system, the proposals would ensure that the total financial rewards to those who work always exceed the benefits given those who do not work.
In addition to provisions for justifiable work-related expenses and compulsory deductions at source, "tax-back" rates for those on support could be reduced to 70 per cent. That is, for every dollar earned, the recipient would keep 30 cents while the remaining 70 cents would go toward reducing the social assistance benefit. Income supplementation would be made available to the most vulnerable members of the working poor-families with children, and singles and couples over 54. It would ensure that they need not fall back into the support system in the face of inadequate returns from employment. Those, such as young single individuals who are better able to increase their earnings through occupational or geographic mobility, would not be eligible for supplementation.
While the benefits available through supplementation are modest by most standards-a maximum of $80 per month for a family of four-they would be a welcome addition to the incomes of families currently struggling hard just to stay afloat. Furthermore, the "tax-back" rate on earnings in supplementation would provide an effective work incentive. For every dollar earned the recipient would keep 65 cents, while the remaining 35 cents would go to reduce the supplementary benefit. Thus the proposals would put in place strong and sensible financial incentives toward work and self-reliance.
These financial incentives would be reinforced by a requirement for periodic employment availability assessment of all recipients of both support and supplementation. To ensure a level of national consistency in this critically important feature of the system, the federal government has put forward a set of guidelines for these assessments. These guidelines require that an assessment be applied to all family units applying for benefits. Furthermore, the assessment would apply to all potential earners within each family, consistent with the objective of distributing available employment among applicant families in such a way as to minimize reliance on public support.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) on bringing before us again today the idea of a guaranteed annual income. I understand that one of his colleagues hopes to be able to say a few words, and therefore I shall keep my remarks brief.
I could not be expected to agree with everything the hon. member said in his interesting speech, but with the main proposal he put forward I am in enthusiastic agreement. I doubt that the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) is aware of what is involved in the concept of a guaranteed annual income otherwise he could hardly have contended that the government side of the House is moving in that direction. The government's review of social security is aimed at ironing out some of the injustices and difficulties which are in our present social security welfare programs, but the guaranteed annual income concept which we hold over here is really an attempt to put society itself on a more just and fairer basis.
As the hon. member for Bellechasse said, what he is asking is that the incomes people have be based on our production as a nation. The basic fact of a society like ours is that the production of wealth is a social process, a social accomplishment. It is not done individualistically any more. It is done by society. The sooner we realize that participation in our society involves the right to be in the work process but also the right to share the goods we produce on a reasonably equal basis, the sooner we will make progress.
We have moved in that direction in a number of ways. Indeed, the best things about our society are the things which we provide universally-education, hospitalization, health care, roads and highways, police and fire protection and those kinds of things, plus pensions on a universal basis to a considerable extent. I look forward to the day when we will have the kind of demogrant which hon. members over here are talking about and which we have been talking about for years. I insist that when that day comes it should be not on a means test basis but on the basis of an allowance that goes to people because they are people, because they are here, because they are part of the Canadian family. If some get too much, let the income tax system then take care of that. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I like the idea that is before us. Let us get started on it soon. If we cannot start it soon for everybody then I should like to see it started soon for veterans. We could then do away with the means tests, the health tests and all the rest. We could say to all veterans over a certain age "Here is your guaranteed income for life."
At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I said I would try to be brief. I welcome this debate. I welcome this idea being thrown open for discussion today. If there are some who say it is futuristic and that it will take a long time to come, like a few others in this House I can say that I have been here long enough to see ideas, which were regarded as impossible when I first came

here, actually realized. I believe Canadians want a better society and that this whole idea of a universal demogrant or a guaranteed income for all our people moves in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, time is running fast and as I want to be brief, I will sum up a little bit.
In February 1976, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) distributed written information on the federal proposals concerning income support and supplementation. On page 6, paragraph (b) of that document, we can read and I quote:
(b) That families drawing support allocations be subject to a minimum 70 per
cent reduction rate on gains, pensions and other incomes from private source.
In other words, every dollar earned would bring about a 70 cents reduction of
the support allocation-
Mr. Speaker, that formula the minister stated last year and which is explained in the brief he submitted to the House of Commons is to penalize people who work and follows the same philosophy as all existing legislation that is to deprive people who work to give to those who do not work. And people are tired of all this, because the one who works is at the same level as the one who does not work. There is hardly any difference between the two people.
That social system, Mr. Speaker, which is widely accepted today is rotten and disastrous for those who work as well as for those who do not work. For instance as we know some people work for a while and when they have enough unemployment stamps they quit and draw unemployment insurance benefits. Then they get another job only to join the unemployed again. They go back to work and once more fall victim to unemployment and the whole thing starts up all over again. At the end of the year, they have worked six months, pay less income tax, received unemployment insurance or welfare benefits while often getting a hidden supplementary income. Most employers nowadays-it is common knowledge-are unable to keep their employees. There is a monthly staff turnover of at least 20 per cent. Every month they must train at least 20 per cent of their personnel who work only long enough to get the number of stamps required to qualify for unemployment insurance.
Moreover, how many workers do we see nowadays who are not the least interested in working overtime because the net salary for overtime is about the same to the net salary for their regular hours because income tax is killing the desire to work. Our current non-social laws are based on such a socialistic mentality. It is bad for the population itself and for the country's economy. If all the unemployed workers and welfare recipients in the country had a guaranteed annual income as advocated today by my colleague, the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert), and as recommended by the Social Crediters in Canada for over 30 years and by a social and non socialistic measure, the difference between a guaranteed annual income as we are proposing today and a redistribution of income and a socialistic formula, our national production could jump by 40 per cent if we put to work all those who are able to work today and are living off unemployment insurance and welfare benefits.
February 7, 1977

With a 40 per cent increase in national production, we would not have to take from the workers to give to those who are not working. Everyone would be better off without the government having to take away from anyone. As he has said on many occasions, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would take from those who have to give to those who are not working anymore and those who do not want to work anymore, so that everyone would be on the same level. He wants to make everyone equally poor.
Mr. Speaker, before beginning to talk about charity in Canada, we should begin by talking about social justice and distribution justice because it is unthinkable to want to do charity when a country does not respect justice first of all because anyone can take from his neighbour to give to charity. Can the country spoliate those who work, in order to give those who have lost the courage to work because of work disincentives? I hope that if and when the Minister of National Health and Welfare tables information on his formula for a guaranteed annual income, his first aim will be social justice rather than social charity. Because there can be no effective social charity in Canada if we do not have first the social justice that would allow someone who earned something through his work to enjoy and retain it.
Mr. Speaker, if the government starts taking away the result of an individual's work to give it to those who would not work because of work disincentives, before long we will have a society where nobody works anymore, where nobody contributes anything to Canada's production and where everyone expects social help, some source of social pittance. Call it welfare allowance, unemployment insurance benefits, Works Canada or what have you. Such programs are work disincentives that in the current economic context induce people to count on some pittance, to live at the government's expense.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe there is a fair amount of ignorance in Canada about our federal social security legislation. A great many people say that the government is trying to assume responsibilities that its own citizens should take unto themselves, that the government should abdicate its paternalistic role. However, there is no real foundation for this belief, since it is almost universally accepted that in some situations people are in definite need of income support and supplementation in addition to social and health services.
The federal government has been reviewing and discussing possible improvements in Canada's welfare system over the past three years. Family allowances, old age security, and the Canada Pension Plan provisions have been modified and improved. Federal-provincial discussions have indicated the need for wages to exceed unemployment insurance or any form of welfare benefits. In other words, though we guarantee a barely adequate income to those who are not working for good reason, we believe that financial incentives should be given
Income Tax Act
those who are employed, thus bolstering our belief in self-reliance and productivity. In fact, by periodic testing of employment availability of recipients of this kind of assistance, we make sure that everyone can participate in the available work to the full level of their capacity.
We propose at this time to provide a program of income support to the aged, the handicapped and to single parent families who cannot work, and also to those for whom no work is available. At the same time, we propose to supplement the incomes of those who receive inadequate pay. This would help the vulnerable members of the working poor, namely, families with children and those over 55 years of age. There are probably half a million families in the country who fall into this category. Some of them would be better off to accept some form of social assistance or welfare; however, their pride keeps them working. Nevertheless, they suffer from a marked economic disadvantage. These citizens on marginal incomes should be encouraged to remain active members of the work force but should have recognition and assistance.
Our intention is to introduce a new social services act during this session, following up the Speech from the Throne. We also intend to make it more desirable to work than to accept welfare. We have support services in mind which are designed to allow the aged, the sick, and the handicapped to live at home rather than in an institution. Meals on wheels, home nursing and homemakers will keep folks in their own community. Rehabilitation will often make the handicapped employable, and assistance in helping them find a job will keep them off welfare. Many people heretofore seemed to be locked into unemployment because if they are handicapped they cannot afford transportation to get to work.

The diversionary tactics which are being used by the Tories prevent me from zeroing in on Bill C-22. If they would only cease their diversionary tactics, we could get on with this debate.
Prior to five o'clock I was raising some relevant points regarding Bill C-22, and I think it is only right, just, and proper that I should remind the House of the points I was raising before the supper hour. We members of the New Democratic Party have not been perverse in the way we have opposed this bill or in the way we have spoken on many clauses of it. We have said over and over again, and we intend to say over and over again during this debate, that a progressive tax system must serve to distribute wealth in Canada, not provide tax loopholes for the well-off. Every single time this government introduces a change with respect to taxation, we end up with loophole upon loophole upon loophole. We on this side of the House are in good company when we say that the tax system is nothing but loophole upon loophole for the well-off. I say that because of what no less a person than Marcel Belanger, president of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, said in a speech to the annual conference of the Canadian Tax Foundation in November, 1975.
I want to put what he said on the record for all hon. members of this House to peruse at their leisure. He said that changes have made Canada's tax system so complicated that even professional tax experts can barely follow it. He asked rhetorically how we can expect the ordinary taxpayer to understand this mess. He urged the federal government to declare a two-year moratorium on tax changes and to concentrate on simplifying the system. He also called for a revision of the income tax rate schedule to ease the burden on lower income Canadians. That is important, Mr. Speaker. He said that governments have modified the tax system time and time again, thus adding to the complications which already exist, and the same time they have unconsciously created loopholes.

Many of these tax changes have failed to produce the intended results, and he cited the registered home ownership savings plan as one example. We have dealt with the registered home ownership savings plan in this debate, and we have pointed out how it is used as a tax loophole for the well-off.
Mr. Belanger pointed out, as we have done in this House, that the RRSP was designed to help young people save in order to buy a house eventually, but it has degenerated into a loophole whereby spouses mutually transfer their property to take advantage of the deduction, and the barefaced aspect of it all is that this is blatantly advertised. Is that what a tax system is all about?
The members of my party have said time and again that the tax system ought to distribute wealth in the country, not accumulate it at the top levels and hope it will filter down. That is the trickle down theory which the government and its allies on the Tory benches have for a long time advocated. Look around, Mr. Speaker. The Liberals and Tories are all products of the trickle down theory. Just look at them. Incidentally, I see that the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton is present. Mr. Belanger went on to say that a straightforward reduction in tax rates would have been simpler and much more effective.
The question which arises is, why not institute a tax rate reduction? Surely that would lead to savings, including savings connected with the bureaucracy of Canada which oversees the RRSP program. I have a sneaking suspicion that RRSPs were set up to help the insurance companies accumulate capital so that they could invest it. I have a sneaking suspicion that that is why the whole program was set up.
It is to help insurance companies invest in shopping plazas.

Yes, so that they can turn round and lend money for the building of sky towers and shopping plazas.
Mr. Belanger went on to say that, as a result of numerous modifications, the federal guide to filing income tax is now 45 pages of small print, the Quebec guide is 41 pages long, and the Ontario guide is 12 pages long. He said that governments have hired actors and performers to convince the little guy that it is simple to fill out his income tax return. Before the poor taxpayer suffers from an inferiority complex he ought to ask those performers, who fills out their income tax returns? Mr. Belanger went on to say that the present income tax rate schedule discourages effort and savings. It has too many brackets. The rates go up too quickly, especially in the lower brackets, and reach too high a level. The federal income tax schedule has 13 levels, he said, more than half of which apply to taxable incomes of less than $10,000. This means that the lower or middle income taxpayer who finds his income increasing because of inflation could easily jump one or even two brackets at a time, thus incurring a proportionately heavier tax burden.

Mr. Belanger went on to suggest that the tax schedule ought to be changed, by cutting the present number of brackets in half, by widening the income classes, and by setting the maximum marginal rate at 38 per cent, instead of as at present, at 47 per cent.
That is the view which I have tried to put forward in the present debate. Mr. Speaker, Mr. Belanger said these things in 1975, and we are now in 1977. It shows that the more things change around here, the more they stay the same. Actually, they deteriorate.
As I was saying earlier this afternoon, tax credits are the most advisable way of distributing wealth in Canada. Some provincial governments have used the tax credit system for social programs. What about the federal government? Has it ever used the tax credit system? The answer is yes. And where has it used the tax credit system? I do not want to be cynical, Mr. Speaker. There are advantages to a tax credit system. We think that since provincial governments have used a tax credit system for social programs, the federal government ought to use that system for its social programs. That is the only fair way of doing it, because then those who earn a buck will pay tax on that buck. As well, a tax credit system could lead to a rationalization of expenditures and a reduction in the numbers of bureaucrats needed to run our present social services system. Clearly there are concrete advantages to a tax credit system. Such a system would be better than the system envisaged by Bill C-22, for we shall need to create a whole new bureaucracy to administer the changes in the act, an act which does nothing but create loophole upon loophole.
Another advantage connected with the tax credit system concerns the establishment of a guaranteed annual income. Surely a tax credit system is one of the best ways of maintaining a guaranteed annual income. It would work to the advantage particularly of those too poor to pay taxes. It could become a negative income tax and that, Mr. Speaker, is in line with our idea of how the tax system of this country should work.

A new income tax provision that allows another avenue for taxfree corporate diversification will be of particular interest to financial institutions.
As part of the general expansion of the sections of the tax law dealing with reorganization, the ability now exists to expand "upstream" without creating any capital gains tax liability.
Tax rules allow taxfree "downstream" diversification, too. But since most financial institutions are not as free as other corporations to diversity through subsidiaries this new rule is an improvement in the tax system for a very large sector of corporate taxpayers.
Surprisingly, the possibility of this type of reorganization has not been widely publicized and Ottawa has not received the credit it should for creating this "government sponsored loophole."

The procedure works as follows:
Company A wishes to create an upstream parent, X; company X is established with no assets. The shareholders of A exchange their shares for treasury shares in X. The shareholders now own X, whose sole assets are the shares of A.

There are, of course, conditions which must be met but these are not unduly restrictive nor unreasonable. The main one is that shareholders in company X must deal at arm's length before the exchange. That is, there must be different directors for the new company, at least temporarily. In addition, no one shareholder may hold more than 50 per cent of X's shares after the exchange.
These restrictions do not affect legitimate business procedures but are designed to prevent owners of closely held corporations avoiding tax.

Once upon a time, and this may sound like a Grimm fairy tale, and in some ways it is, in the halcyon days of the sixties, the predecessor of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the late Lester B. Pearson, went to a man named Carter. He said Carter-

The point 1 was trying to make is that while this gives much spiritual comfort to the soul, it has been the rationale for parts of Atlantic Canada that we have always offered spiritual solace. The rulers of the country are the people who sit in judgment. Here we are sitting in judgment on Bill C-22. We have to make a decision on it. It seems to me that if there were some meekness in the hearts of the government, some righteousness and some mercy, they would not attempt to foist on the people of Canada a bill such as Bill C-22.
There is cynicism in the land. Some would put that cynicism down to experiences south of the border, and I suppose that is a good rationale. They have a right to be cynical, however, about the things they see in the government of Canada today. First, the government ends the freeze it imposed last year on the cost of living index for family allowances. Since the allowance is taxable, families at different income levels get to keep different proportions of the increase. Thus a family of two earning $10,000 will retain $32 of it, while the same size family with a $50,000 income only retains $21. To compensate the $50,000 a year family for getting $11 less benefit from the allowance boost, the government is going to give an extra $593 by abolishing the 10 per cent surtax on incomes of more than $30,000. Increasing family allowances will cost the government $115 million. That's $165 million it will pay out, less than $50 million it will tax back. Cancelling the surtax will cost $135 million. As for chiropractors their average salary went from $27,500 to $29,100, an increase of $1,600, or in percentage terms 5.8 per cent. Consultants: their salaries went from $16,700 to $17,800, an increase of $1,100, or a percentage change of 6.6 per cent. Dentists; their base income went from $34,100 to $40,800, an increase of $6,700, or 19.6 per cent. That is almost three times as much as the supposed limit under the anti-inflation guidelines. I doubt whether the excess was ever collected. Engineers: their salaries went from $38,200 to $45,900, an increase of $7,700 or 20.2 per cent. As for lawyers-
Shhhhhh!
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) is shushing me.
No, I am not.

Lawyers went from $34,900 to $40,000, an increase of $5,100, or 14.6 per cent. The salaries of optome-
February 7, 1977

trists went from $29,000 to $31,600, an increase of $2,600, or 9 per cent. Salaries of public accountants went from $38,500 to $42,700, an increase of $4,200 or 10.9 per cent. Veterinarians: their salaries went from $25,100 to $26,500, an increase of $1,400, or 5.6 per cent. Doctors' salaries went from $45,700 to $49,000, an increase of $3,300, or 7.2 per cent. The average increase, Mr. Speaker, was from a base of $35,700 to $40,600, an average change in dollars of $4,900, and the average percentage change is 13.7 per cent.
What kind of game is being played here, Mr. Speaker? Every time the government permits a tax change, it is imposing it upon Figures and facts of this kind. This can only serve to heighten the disparities within the system. It gives it a warp and makes it unfair and unjust for people at the bottom end of the income ladder.
When implementing these tax changes from whom is the government asking a sacrifice? Who is the government asking to make a contribution to the national good and the national welfare of our country? Is it going to be Mr. Beaulieu, who washes cars for $8,000 a year or is it going to be that lady in my riding office who earns $7,900 a year? Who will it be? Will it be Mr. Albert Thornborough, the president of Massey-Ferguson Limited, who made $353,662 last year? My, but there is some restraint there! Last week I wanted to know how one man can earn $353,662 a year. The sky's the limit, and all we ever do is open up the floodgates so that more taxes can be written off, taxes which should be paid to this country. Mr. Thornborough ought to be proud to live in Canada, and he ought to learn to pay his fair share of taxes, but when he has handmaidens sitting over there, and when his mouthpieces support him over on this side every time a tax change is proposed, the Albert Thornboroughs of this world-
Order!

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. On second thought I wonder if we should not consider allowing the hon. member to go back to the Bible. I am also curious about the time limit of the hon. member. He started at 4.20 this afternoon. I am a bit curious as to how much longer we have to suffer through this.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: For the information of the hon. member, I think the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) is allowed to talk as long as he wishes. He is the first spokesman at third reading.

The hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) ought to relax because I am getting to the Old Testament. I particularly like some quotations from Genesis, and tomorrow I am going to quote from the Old Testament because it is very relevant to the Income Tax Act. We know that Matthew, whose name was Levi, was a publican. He was a tax collector, and he put more taxes into his pocket than he did into the church collection. Does that sound familiar? By golly, Bill C-22-
Income Tax Act
You are going to be struck by lightning if you keep that up.

-is highly reminiscent of what had to be done to those moneychangers and tax collectors. They had to be cleaned out. Fortunately, we have abandoned capital punishment, and we are on the way to abandoning corporal punishment, so we cannot whip them any more. However, that might be a good idea.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: We haven't done away with corporal punishment.

I am always very happy when hon. members interject because, when they do that, and rise on points of order, I know that the points I am making are really getting under their skin. I can understand the hon. member for Restigouche coming to the rescue of Mr. Thornborough, coming from a riding like his which has unemployment of over 30 per cent. He would like to defend a person who earns $353,662. He should be ashamed of himself.
How much longer are you going to hold up the House?
Who cares?

Who else is being asked to contribute? Will it be a chap by the name of Borje Salming, a Toronto Maple Leaf hockey player, who makes $250,000 a year? Will it be H. R. Fraser, the chairman of Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting, who makes $160,000 a year? Will it be CTV news anchorman Lloyd Robertson, who makes $100,000 a year? Will it be Eric Trigg, the executive vice-president of Alcan Aluminum Limited, who in 1974 received a salary of $147,438 and in 1975 received a salary of $162,178, an increase of 10 per cent?
Oh, oh!

Oh, but they are squealing now. All their Tory friends are being named. Will it be John Armstrong, chairman of the board and president of Imperial Oil, who made $234,333 in 1975, $36,000 more than in 1974? Will it be Clifford Hatch, president of Hiram-Walker-Gooderham and Worts Limited, who earned a salary of $225,000 last year? Will it be A. E. Feldmeyer, president and managing director of Canadian Superior Limited, who received a salary of $311,400 last year?
Will it be John Devlin, chairman of the board of Carling-O'Keefe Limited, who received a salary of $164,829? Will it be Edgar M. Bronfman, chairman of the board of Seagram's Company, who made a salary of $300,000 last year? Will it be Sandy Holly, a jockey, who made $450,000 last year? He is a racehorse jockey, not a disc jockey. At one end of the spectrum we have these corporate wheels.
I would like to know the yardstick by which one man can earn $350,000 or $450,000 and take advantage of many loopholes besides. For these people it is like the gates of Jerusalem opening. There is a new Jerusalem for them. But

February 7, 1977
Income Tax Act
what about the other end of the scale, where Mr. Beaulieu, working 60 hours a week in a cold, wet, damp and dank car wash, makes $8,600 a year? Surely if the government has its priorities right and if its head is screwed on properly, the verses I quoted, Matthew chapter 5, verses 1-16, have some relevance to the whole question of justice, meekness, and getting something back from the tax system.
When were you ever meek?

If hon. members want to make comments, they can speak when they get the floor, whenever that may be. I do not know when they will get the floor, but when they do, they can get up and make a speech. The wraps were put on the hon. member. He has to keep his mouth shut.
To add to this immense inequality, Bill C-22 does not contain a single clause which recognizes that the tax burden is being shifted from the corporate tax to personal income tax. From 1970 to 1975 the effective rate of corporate tax on profits went down from 29.6 per cent to 26.6 per cent, and did hon. members ever hear them squeal louder? And what do they want now? They want tax breaks. They are all wanting more concessions. Mining companies want more write-offs. They want more of everything. That is the kind of solution they seek. And here we have the government bringing in a bill which does nothing to deal with this inequitable situation.
We have shifted the corporate tax burden to the individual taxpayer and while doing so corporate profits have skyrocketed from $7.7 billion to $17.8 billion. Add to that the fact that the Anti-Inflation Board, which is controlling wages, allowed an unspecified number of corporations to exceed AIB guidelines by $70 million in the first six months of the program. Corporate taxes were cut this year by 1 per cent, as was the case last year, the year before, and the year before that.
There has been a corporate tax cut every year since 1972 so that today the corporate tax rate has been reduced to 46 per cent from 50 per cent in 1972. This, of course, is not the actual rate at which most corporations paid tax; that is a little closer to 27 per cent, Mr. Speaker. The other tax concessions made notorious by David Lewis in his 1972 election campaign are still being enjoyed by the same corporate welfare bums. In fact they have both hands in our pockets now. It is indeed unfortunate that the present government, aided and abetted by the Tory opposition, has conned, and I can use no other word-has conned the middle class of this country into believing that the economic woes of this nation are caused by a working class that is alternately greedy, grasping, lazy, dishonest and unconscientious. Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of thing it would want us to believe.
I often become cynical, and I have to admit this. I share the same cynicism that large numbers of Canadians have. 1 have to be ashamed of it. But do you know what makes me cynical, Mr. Speaker? My experience in Canada is short for I am not a native born Canadian-just a lowly little immigrant who went to teach school in the backwoods of Ontario. However, when I
[Mr Rodriguez.]
look at the tax system I cannot think of any group of people for whom taxes on part of their incomes are waived but members of parliament.
Don't get nasty now.

This party has argued against that kind of elitist attitude. I have to call a spade a spade, Mr. Speaker. We have argued the principle that a buck is a buck is a buck and should be taxed. Members of parliament are now getting 10,600 bucks on which they pay no tax. Is it any wonder people in Canada are looking askance at members of parliament and becoming cynical, like me? What do they say to themselves? They ask how different we are from them. They have expenses too but cannot write them off. They have to pay taxes on everything they earn. This party has said there should not be an amount allowed as expenses; it should all be wages and be taxed.
I become even more cynical when it comes to making arrangements about what is going to come under the antiinflation controls. That was always dumped on the non-taxable part. That is what the cynicism is all about. Every member has to stand up before his constituents and be honest with them, but how can we say we approve and advocate a fair taxation system? I know it is open season on Liberals in this country today, but that is another story that I have to deal with tomorrow sometime.
People are cynical about governments today that pass that kind of tax law. How quickly we could move to taxfree moneys for members of parliament, and look how long it takes to get old age pensions indexed! The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stands up in this House constantly and makes the argument for veterans' widows and widows 60 years of age.
It really hurts, Mr. Speaker. That is why I quoted from Matthew because it is relevant to what we are doing in this House. We pray every day before we start question period, but what does it all mean? We are just like those publicans in the Old Testament and the New Testament: we collect taxes and put them in our own pockets but do not put enough in the church poor box. That is what it is all about.
I get these black moments, but I come out of them pretty quickly, Mr. Speaker. As I was saying before, if we were to look at the percentages of tax payable to this government by the individual and corporate sectors the figures would show that the burden of taxation has been shifting from the corporate sector on to the individual in spite of all the froofraro, and public relations, and free enterprise, and all that sort of thing.
I get cynical about other things that I notice as well. I have here something handed out by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) called the Advisory Committee Annual Report, 1976. It contains exactly four pages on the work of a corporation that spent $3Vt billion last year. I do not know how much this report costs. We cannot find money for people at the bottom end of the income scale but we can find money for four pages of nonsense supposedly reporting on a
February 7, 1977

corporation that spent $31/2 billion. They should put their heads in a bag in shame.
Never let it be said that the Liberals are not concerned about redistributing wealth in this country. They are never at a loss, but always flim-flam and whitewash a situation, and come up with something that takes the heat off the particular problem of the moment. I know they are concerned with income redistribution and they have come up with a unique way of doing it. Never let it be said they lack creativity or panache. They thought and thought about it, and came up with a national lottery. Some men in Montreal had a highfalutin' idea about the Olympics and ran up a billion dollar debt, and here is the solution-a lottery.
It was touched on in an article written by Russell Mills, editor of the Ottawa Citizen, on February 5, entitled "Lottery's Sweet Temptation Merely a Tax on Stupidity". He writes:
We've got to stop these whining do-gooders before they take away our lotteries. Their campaign is heating up.
This week a Toronto psychiatrist said that the unrealistic expectation of winning could be dangerous psychologically and that the lotteries were creating a generation of gamblers in Canada. Others maintain that they undermine the work ethic.
And there have always been those who claim that lotteries are a tax on the poor because many tickets are bought by desperate people.
But lotteries aren't really a tax on the poor, they're a tax on stupidity. And although it is true that a large number of the stupid do find themselves at the bottom of the economic heap they're not at all in the higher social classes.
Lotteries are a very effective way of isolating the stupid since with the absurdly low chances of winning that they offer, no one with a brain larger than an acorn would even consider buying a lottery ticket.
With the present odds, on Loto Canada, for example, you would have to spend $100,000 a year on tickets for 36 years-a total of $3.6 million, not including interest on the money-before you would even have a 50-50 chance of winning a $1 million prize. Who but a twit would buy a ticket at those odds?
That's precisely why our present lotteries are hopelessly inadequate and should be expanded and promoted far more than they are today.
How else are we going to get the stupid to pay their fair share of running the country?
Look at what they are costing us. The stupid are the ones who smoke and drink too much, don't exercise, don't wear seat belts, smoke in bed and drink and drive and thus add enormous amounts to our health costs.
They are the ones who drop out of school and then can't find jobs, run off and leave families without support, go bankrupt, quit their jobs or get fired and then expect us to support them with unemployment insurance or welfare.
Because most of the stupid don't make much money, they don't pay much in taxes, not nearly enough to pay for the trouble they cause.
Outside of a major slash in government services, the only way we can hope to reduce the cost of stupidity is to harness it, with lotteries. Because there's one thing about the stupid-they love to throw away their money.
But government promotion of the lotteries has been shamefully inadequate.
The average Canadian only spends $40 a year on lottery tickets now compared to an average of $150 a person in Britain and more than $200 in Japan.
With a little clever promotion this spending could be increased 10 times or more.
The advertising should take dead aim on the stupid and seek them out wherever they may be.
There should be lottery advertising included with all welfare and unemployment insurance cheques.
Income Tax Act
And no more of this namby-pamby 'lifestyle' advertising that the do-gooders are so upset about, let's use straight guilt and hit the thick right where it hurts.
How about this for the insert with welfare cheques:
Are you feeling bad because your family eats macaroni seven days a week? When did they last have steak ? Do the other children laugh at the holes in their clothes? Give them a shot at a better life. Buy a Loto Canada ticket today!
Or how about this inserted with UIC cheques:
So you've lost your job. Do you realize that the unemployment rate is over seven per cent today and shows no signs of going down? You may never work again. Winning the lottery may be the only way out. You'd better buy a ticket!
Try guilt appeal.
All beer parlours and cheap bars should be saturated with guilt advertising and all waiters and bartenders paid commissions to push tickets on drunks.
Feeling guilty because you're drinking up the paycheque again? Taking food out of the kiddies' mouths? Give them a chance. Buy a lottery ticket along with the next round!
Hard-hitting lottery promotions should also be placed at other haunts of the dumb; on all cigarette machines, on bottles of Canadian sherry, at professional hockey games and horse-racing tracks and in all CB radio shops.
The ultimate aim should be to make enough profit from these tickets to pay for all government services. Then taxes could be reduced to zero and those of us too bright to chase the illusion of instant wealth could pursue our pleasures unimpeded by the burden of taxation.
It's all a matter of promotion. And for an advertising industry that can sell platform shoes, genital deodorants and electric shoebrushes, it should be a snap.
Lotteries apparently are the panacea for all our ills. We now have the Olympic lottery, the Ontario lottery, Loto Canada and the Quebec lottery. Lotteries, clearly, are the new wave.
We said, when we debated national lotteries in this country, that if part of the money derived from the national lottery were to be used for important programs like amateur sport and for health building programs, those activities ought to be supported under a budgetary provision and paid for with taxes collected from all Canadians working and earning a buck. That is the principle we have advocated consistently. We say a buck is a buck and should be taxed when it is earned. That principle this government has shied away from, for it wants to help its friends in the board rooms of Bay Street, Toronto, and St. Catharines Street in Montreal. 1 could even touch on who gets the distributorships for lotteries, but that is another subject with which I will not deal tonight. I can deal with it on Friday, when I return to this question. It seems to me that is a horse of a different colour.
I have talked about loopholes created in our tax laws. Lotteries are to be the substitute for a fair taxation system. While the government taxes the poor through lotteries, it subsidizes the rich with loopholes and reductions in tax. I have already talked about this, but it cannot be emphasized too much. If I am open to the charge that I repeat myself, I cannot help it.
Let us look at the question of interest earned in Canada. It is true that anyone earning interest income from investments can deduct the first $1,000 of such income before computing taxable income. But who uses that system? Who benefits? Each of the three million Canadians earning incomes of between $4,000 and $8,000 saved, on average, $35 from this provision. Yet each of the 225,000 people in the $25,000 to $50,000 category managed to save, on average, $216 in taxes, for a total of $49 million of unneeded tax breaks. That was the

February 7, 1977
Income Tax Act
extent of the tax break to higher income brackets. They saved $49 million. There were 13 times more people in lower tax brackets, but their total tax saved was only twice that saved by people in the higher tax bracket. Yes, their total tax saving was only twice as large as that of the group at the top. In other words, this provision is heavily weighted in favour of the top brackets, precisely because they have disposable income to invest.
The point is that, for the $550 million total cost of the tax program to the treasury, the government could have increased family allowances by over 25 per cent, doubled the annual increase in the old age pension, or offered a substantial tax credit to those at the bottom of the income scale. But the Liberals did not want to do it that way. Instead they decided to distribute their largesse at the top.
Let us consider another tax gimmick. Our whole tax system is strewn with gimmickry. I said before that it is full of loopholes. I suppose the government can get away with it because lower income people are not able to comprehend the fine print in the income tax system. The gimmick to which I am referring is known as the Registered Home Ownership Plan, better known as RHOP. It was supposed to help moderate income people afford a house. It was supposed to help young people to save toward the purchase of a home. And how many people have used the program? Of those earning between $5,000 and $6,000 only one in 95 has used it. That is, just over 1 per cent of those people managed to sock away money under this program in 1974. They just did not have money to put away. But at the other end of the income scale, and I am speaking of people in the over $50,000 bracket most of whom own their own homes already and are thus ineligible, over 6 per cent took advantage of this gimmick. That is the crux of the point we are trying to make about this bill.
In effect, here was a program which, on the surface, was designed to help people to save for a house. That was commendable. Then the authorities said that if you already own your own home you can transfer ownership to your spouse's name. Then you can start collecting under the program and be eligible for the benefits and write-offs under the tax system. It is not fair. I just pointed out that six times as many people in the $50,000 and over bracket were able to take advantage of the benefits in 1974. If the minister and the government think that this is an effective means of helping the low income earners afford homes, they are just whistling Dixie. They are not telling it like it is.
Again with regard to this gimmick, the benefits are highly weighted in favour of top income earners. Let us not forget the spousal Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. A home is registered in the name of one spouse or the other. One of them can put away $1,000 of non-taxable income for a future investment in furniture or another home. This was commented on by Marcel Belanger whom I quoted earlier in my speech this evening. He is quoted in the November 22, 1975, edition of the Financial Post.
That's old.

It may be old, but the same loophole is there. The government is talking about a fair taxation system. The reason I quoted from Matthew is because we are talking about justice and fair play. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Stevens) has the gall to say that is a fair tax proposal. The Bay Street barons may think so, but not those in northern Ontario whom I and other members of this House represent.
What Marcel Belanger said about the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan is still applicable today. He said, and I quote:
Let's take the case of the Registered Home Ownership Plan. It was designed to help young couples save in order to eventually buy a house; it has degenerated into a loophole where spouses mutually transfer their property, should circumstances so require, to take advantage of the deduction.
There is a strange morality about that!
Immorality.

It is not doing anything illegal, merely taking advantage of a loophole which has been permitted by the government. If the tax on the $1,000 is not paid because of a spousal transfer, the rest of the population must pick up the deficit. That is not fair by any stretch of the imagination, even using Liberal or Conservative logic. There is not a member in this House, even those who make their remarks from behind the curtains, who is prepared to argue that is a fair proposal. That is why we are dead set against this bill and have argued against this particular clause.
There are other juicy loopholes in this bill. Let us not think that they are only limited to the federal income tax structure.
The province of Ontario came out with a $1,500 house grant. Who was the first in line applying for a grant on a $108,000 home in Carp? It was the Conservative member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek). He received a $1,500 house grant on a $108,000 house. Surely that is not the purpose of the Ontario scheme. As a matter of fact, the Ontario minister responsible for this program, Arthur Meen, said that he is prepared to write off all those who rip off the system. If someone were to take the unemployment insurance fund to the cleaners, they would not write that off. They would hound him to the ground. However, here we have a well-to-do Tory member of parliament receiving a grant on a $108,000 home. This well-heeled minister without portfolio in the shadow cabinet is taking money right out of the hands of the poor people of Ontario. It is for this reason I quoted Matthew 5: 1-16 which talks about justice and fair play. Hon. members should spend more time reading and contemplating that.
We then come to half taxation on capital gains. The story is the same. When capital gains were brought in, we heard a great squealing. Even though it was only to be on 50 per cent of the gain, the Tories were squealing and squirming. They said it would take away all incentive. In fact the only policy that party has enunciated is that they would return to the 100 per cent tax free on capital gains.

February 7, 1977
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) accept a question?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, when 1 am finished my address to the House I will certainly permit a question. However, I cannot say when that will be. I have a lot of material and many ideas to present. It looks now as though I will take until Friday. Possibly some time between 4.30 and 5 o'clock on Friday I will permit a question, no later because 1 have a flight to catch. However, at this point I would like to continue because I have some very precise comments. They might interest the hon. member. In fact they may lead to some more questions.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a further point of order.
I believe the hon. member misunderstood me. I believe he would Find my question most helpful if he would give me an opportunity to put it. Perhaps he could give an answer that would be of great interest to the members of this House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Again, the Chair must seek permission from the hon. member for Nickel Belt. Will the hon. member accept a question?

Since the hon. member puts it that way, and as I am not a hard person to get along with, 1 do not mind him asking a question at this time. I have thought about it and the hon. member can ask his question.

After listening to the hon. member for two hours and 20 minutes I wish to ask him out of curiosity whether he can tell us of any country in the world that has a tax system which he feels is ideal? If so, will he mention the name of that country so we can perhaps take a look at it?

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question, that has always been the approach of Tory governments in the past. They look outside the borders of Canada for models which do not necessarily Fit Canadian needs. Our party has come up with a taxation system that is fair and just. It follows the recommendations of the Carter Commission report. I do not know whether the hon. member was in the Chamber an hour and 20 minutes ago when I dealt with the Carter Commission report. Surely the hon. member cannot argue with the premise that a buck is a buck is a buck and it should be taxed when it is earned.
The next point in our program concerns tax credits. By using tax credits we could move toward what we have always called the GAI program.
The Gay program?

The guaranteed annual income program. We are not looking for a Shangri La outside Canada. We have the resources and the ability to enable us to build a tax system
Income Tax Act
which meets our needs. In the United States today they are looking for ways to revise the tax system-
Tell us about what they are doing in Russia.

The hon. member for York-Simcoe is holding up the example of the Russian model. That is a very conservative model. That is state capitalism. He would be good as a commissioner on financial matters in the central committee. And do you know something, Mr. Speaker? He would not look out of place in that line-up. Get him a uniform, get him a cap, get him the order of Lenin-the hon. member for Water-loo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) brought several of those back-and he could take his place on the reviewing stand. He would Fit in. But we who believe in democracy and freedom of choice could never accept such a system.
What about the U.K., then?

As to the United Kingdom, I would point out again to the hon. member that we must use Canadian talent, Canadian resources to build a tax system of a kind which meets our needs. And we who support the New Democratic Party would not come up with these fly-by-night programs such as the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. We would outline a housing policy based on housing as a social need, which is more than the official opposition and their new leader have been able to do; he has been going around the country talking about the Conservatives as an alternative government, but they do not have an alternative policy, so how could they form an alternative government?
The story is the same when it comes to the capital gains tax, even though the rate is 50 per cent. The Tories rushed to oppose it. One would think it threatened to take away all the wealth from those they favour. We have found out since that those with income of $20,000 or more made an average of $1,056 in capital gains in 1974, half of which was untaxed, for a total cost to the treasury of $148 million.
At the other end of the scale, the 4.3 million people getting between $4,000 and $10,000 registered an average capital gain of $14 for a total of $13 million. This is what we have been criticizing. We have been saying that our tax system, our model, would not contain loopholes. We have shown conclusively that no less than $6 billion was lost because of these loopholes. Somebody has to pick up that amount. Just imagine what would happen if all of us took advantage of the loopholes. Who would be carrying the tax burden? Somebody has to pay.
The workers.

Every time I think about work I am reminded of the industrial freedom songs I learnt when I was in school. We had them put in a little red book long before we ever heard of Chairman Mao's little red book. One, in particular, is appropriate. Since the hon. member for York-Simcoe is interested in the Soviet model, I think he will be interested in this song. It goes:
Why don't you work like other men do?
How in Hell can I work when there's no work to do?

Even education costs are going up, and we hear that only the children of the rich will be able to go to universities. subtopic: ENERGY-PARTICIPATION IN MARITIME ENERGY POOL AND CONSTRUCTION OF GENERATING PLANTS
ENERGY-PARTICIPATION IN MARITIME ENERGY POOL AND CONSTRUCTION OF GENERATING PLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 25 I raised again with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) a theme I voiced in a speech in this House on May 4, 1976, that of a maritime energy pool to make development of electric and transmitting facilities a priority and achieve maximum economies of scale with resultant benefit to all maritime users of electric energy.
I feel strongly that this is the course to follow and that the minister should give leadership in this direction. Dramatic increases in the cost of electric power in areas of Atlantic Canada have placed the region at a competitive disadvantage in the expansion of its industrial and manufacturing sectors, and inflicted a great measure of hardship on large segments of the population. We live with the fact that Atlantic Canada will continue to import over 100 million barrels of oil per year to sustain its energy systems. A carefully planned pool of generation and distribution systems would achieve vastly improved economies of scale. Strong interconnection with adjacent areas of Canada and the U.S.A. would optimize power pool benefits.
[Mr. Rodriguez.)
These proposals are not new. Speaking in this House in May of last year I put forward similar suggestions. However, the government has done little about the situation, and now I find myself, once again, asking that something be done.
The challenge of meeting future energy requirements at a reasonable cost is one which cannot and should not be met by the Atlantic provinces individually. Co-ordination and co-operation are imperative if this goal is to be achieved. The provinces are interested. The federal government should provide the enlightened leadership and the imagination necessary for the implementation of such inter-governmental schemes. Until Ottawa can come up with a plan, long overdue, to assist in the setting up of a maritime power pool, the people of Atlantic Canada will suffer through bleak and expensive winters.
The government cannot abrogate its responsibility any longer. It is not enough to express interest and polite approval. The scheme deserves an investment which can pay great dividends: active leadership and a commitment of financial support.
