subtopic: ENERGY-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO INCREASE EXPLORATION IN FRONTIER AREAS
ENERGY-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO INCREASE EXPLORATION IN FRONTIER AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of alarming reports in regard to the possibility of an energy shortage which would seriously affect all Canadians, I should like to register my concern over the government's lack of a clear energy policy. The recent report of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development has called for new government policies for conservation and energy development to head off shortages, but I wonder whether the government of Canada has taken heed. The government of Canada has a moral obligation to answer the question: how are we going to meet our energy needs, and to what extent?
For the record, Mr. Speaker, the OECD has urged its members, Canada included, to develop additional energy supplies by implementing such policies as providing incentives for improvements in oil recovery and support programs. Measures to increase production should be aimed at improving the climate for investment. That certainly is not the case at present in Canada. In many respects the government is hindering development through excessive regulations. The reaction of the government to energy problems has been to regulate. Virtually every aspect of the Canadian petroleum industry is

now tightly regulated. Canadians should really be concerned that one of our major industries is subject to regulations that are often unstable, unclear, and unco-ordinated to the point where the industry's performance is impaired.
The government must take a great deal of the blame for Canada's energy problems. Rather than assisting the oil industry by working in a spirit of co-operation on a problem that is vital to our nation, this government has put obstacles in the way of developing a positive energy policy.
The question of energy policy in the present and the future is among the most important issues facing Canada at this time. To most Canadians, energy policy is wrapped up in pricing- what we pay for home heating, electricity, of at the gasoline puihps. The government cannot hide from the fact that there is an energy shortage, and Canadians want to know what it intends to do about it. In 1974, Canada ceased being a net crude oil exporter. In 1975, Canada imported an average of 115 million barrels of crude oil per day. While Canada still exports 39 per cent of its natural gas production, this is expected to decline in the mid-1980's and create a serious balance of payments problem. Even by 1980 Canada is forecast to spend over $3 billion yearly for imported oil. Forecasts show the situation becoming progressively worse in the 1980's.
In addition to hindering the energy problem through excessive regulations, the government has also taken a large portion of revenue from the oil industry which could well be used in expanding the oil industry to meet rising energy demands. It must be pointed out that by far the greatest bulk of price increases in oil of late have resulted from increased government taxes. For instance, fully 60 per cent of the cost of a gallon of gas at the pump is federal, provincial of municipal tax. Only 38 per cent of the cost covers the oil itself, its refining, marketing, the dealer's wage, etc. Profit is approximately 2 per cent of the price. I for one reject the idea that the oil industry is enjoying excessive profits. The oil industry today is in worse position than it was prior to the fall of 1973. when the wellhead price of a barrel of crude oil was $3.
Taxes and royalties now consume, for example, about $6 of the $9.75 for a barrel of Alberta crude oil. After taxes, Mr. Speaker, the oil companies have little left for oil exploration and development. What can be said with certainty is that oil exploration costs are skyrocketing, not just because of inflation but because today drilling is at expensive sites since cheaper sites have already been explored. Returns from money invested in oil exploration are quite low compared to other investment opportunities. This too has discouraged investment in exploration. On top of all of that oil company profits are quite variable due to the uncertain nature of production.
While the energy problem continues to become serious, many Canadians are wondering what the government intends to do. Should we satisfy our energy needs from our own resources to the full extent possible at costs that offer Canada an economic advantage? I think most Canadians would answer yes, and yet the government is showing no leadership in developing such a policy. I would guarantee that our energy
Adjournment Debate
needs are met and mitigate the risks associated with massive oil imports.
As we all know, oil is a non-renewable resource. Canada's energy priorities should include an effort to minimize our use of energy. Producing our own energy resources where the costs are right may offer tremendous economic savings and benefits, but wringing out the waste in our use of energy offers even greater economic savings and benefits. Simply stated, our energy conservation objective should be the use of the minimum amount of energy required to meet our social and economic needs and aspirations. Conservation, however, cannot answer all of our energy needs.
In terms of the many challenges which today confront Canada, energy is only one challenge, but it will have inevitable effects on all the others. While there are no easy nor instant solutions to our energy challenge, that is not an excuse for the government to ignore the problem and drift along hoping the problem will solve itself.
As I stated earlier, the government has a moral obligation to answer the question of how we are going to meet our energy needs. If it does have a long range contingency plan, then it should be made public. Canadians will not tolerate secrecy on such a vital matter. I rather suspect, however, that it is not a case of secrecy but rather of no policy. I would urge the government to develop a clear policy for energy before it is too late.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the often raised questions from my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie), I should say, on top of what the minister and I have already said with regard to many of these interesting questions that, as regards the special revenues from oil and gas production that the federal government is collecting from the motor gasoline exise tax and from the oil export tax, these funds are specifically designated to maintain the oil import compensation fund to equalize gasoline prices across Canada and are not part of general revenues. As regards the prevailing financial environment, the hon. member should be aware of the incentive nature of the government's federal corporate tax system as related to the mineral resources industries.
Furthermore, as has been pointed out in the House before, it is the government's intention to monitor both the volume of cash flows accruing to the petroleum industry and the level of expenditures made by the industry in the search for new energy supplies. This monitoring will be conducted by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and will provide the government with the information it needs to ensure that industry is using its increased revenues to respond to the country's need for new oil and gas resources.
In the statement of policy on a proposed petroleum and natural gas act and new Canada oil and gas land regulations tabled in the House on May 19, 1976, by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), he stated that the principles embodied in the legislation governing frontier
